Building the Book
To build the notes locally, clone the repository and use a Python 3.12 virtual environment of your choice. With uv, run these commands from a terminal:
git clone https://github.com/statds/ids-book.git
cd ids-book
uv venv --python 3.12 /path/to/your/environment
source /path/to/your/environment/bin/activate
make install
make check
make render
If uv is unavailable, replace the uv venv command with python3.12 -m venv and use the same path. If you already have an appropriate activated environment, run make install directly. The install target uses the active environment; make check verifies the required tools; and make render writes the completed book to _book/index.html. Supply any credentials required by particular examples through documented local configuration, and never commit credentials or generated output to Git.
Quarto writes the rendered book to _book/. Generated output and local caches are not tracked by Git; the source and environment specifications are.

title: Introduction to Data Science
section: Learning Data Science in the Age of AI
text:
Learning Data Science in the Age of AI
AI reduces the value of routine analytical production but increases the value of analytical judgment. AI systems can already write routine code, clean data, create visualizations, fit models, and draft reports. Consequently, a course that consists mainly of memorizing commands or reproducing standard analyses would offer diminishing value. The appropriate response is not to abandon data-science education, but to teach the knowledge and judgment needed to use increasingly capable tools well.
Current labor evidence shows disruption and demand at the same time. In its 2025 survey, the World Economic Forum reported that 41 percent of employers expected to reduce their workforce where AI could automate tasks, while 77 percent planned to upskill their workers. The same report identified AI and big data as the fastest-growing skill area and analytical thinking as the most widely valued core skill (World Economic Forum, 2025). In the United States, the Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment of data scientists to grow by about 34 percent from 2024 to 2034 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Such projections are not a promise of a job, but they do show why students need a combination of technical knowledge and analytical judgment rather than less preparation.
AI tends to amplify the capabilities of its user rather than make expertise irrelevant. A person with limited understanding may use AI to produce a weak analysis faster, more confidently, and in more polished language. A strong researcher can use the same technology to investigate more alternatives, challenge assumptions, detect errors, and undertake work that would previously have required much more time. The difference is not merely skill in writing prompts. It is the ability to conceive, direct, and evaluate an analysis.
First, students need enough knowledge to recognize what is possible. A useful analysis begins before any code is written: someone must connect a substantive problem to data that could inform it, distinguish descriptive, predictive, causal, and decision questions, and recognize promising methods. Without this foundation, a user can ask AI only for familiar tasks and may not notice when a question cannot be answered from the available data. Knowledge expands both the range and the ambition of what a student can imagine doing.
Second, students must learn how to direct AI. A vague real-world concern must be translated into precise questions, variables, comparisons, and computational steps. The user must supply context, state constraints, decide what evidence would be relevant, and revise the approach as new problems emerge. These are central data-science skills. AI can assist with their execution, but it cannot compensate reliably for a poorly formulated problem.
Third, students must be able to evaluate what AI produces. Plausible code may contain subtle errors; an attractive graph may conceal a misleading comparison; a highly accurate model may suffer from data leakage; and a fluent report may make a causal claim that the study design cannot support. Evaluation therefore requires understanding data provenance, measurement, variation, validation, uncertainty, reproducibility, and the context in which a result will be used. Because AI can make incorrect work appear polished and authoritative, these foundations become more important, not less.
This course prepares students to work with AI without surrendering judgment to it. Students learn enough about data, computation, statistical reasoning, and communication to formulate worthwhile questions, supervise computational work, verify results, explain limitations, and take responsibility for the conclusions they present. The goal is not to compete with AI at producing code quickly. It is to become the kind of informed practitioner whose abilities are made stronger by AI.

title: Introduction to Data Science
text:
Adapting to Rapid Skill Acquisition
Data science requires learning new tools and ideas quickly. VanderPlas (VanderPlas, 2016) emphasizes that effective practice depends less on memorizing every command than on locating and evaluating the information needed to solve an unfamiliar problem.
Effective practitioners follow a disciplined process for resolving unfamiliar problems. They frame the problem, consult documentation and other reliable sources, test possible solutions, and evaluate whether the result makes sense.
This habit is especially important when software, data formats, and computing environments change. Encountering an unfamiliar package, error message, data source, or hardware requirement is part of the work. The goal is to develop a repeatable way to investigate such problems rather than to accumulate isolated recipes.

title: Introduction to Data Science
text:
Working Principles
The examples and exercises in this book emphasize a few recurring principles:

Begin with a domain concern or available data, then formulate a clear question in context.
Keep raw data separate from derived data and analysis output.
Explore data interactively, then collect tested code into reproducible scripts or documents.
Consider during data cleaning how each variable will be used later.
Use version control to make small, understandable changes.
Document data sources, assumptions, software dependencies, and decisions.
Check results for statistical, computational, and contextual plausibility.
Communicate the question, evidence, limitations, and conclusion—not merely the code.

Effective presentations guide the audience from motivation to conclusion. Introduce the problem and explain why it matters, provide a map of the talk, emphasize the main results, and conclude with the central takeaway.
Trustworthy explanations distinguish original work from borrowed material. Original examples strengthen an explanation, while careful attribution allows the audience to evaluate its sources.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 What Is Data Science?
Data science is the practice of learning from data. It combines statistical reasoning, computation, and knowledge of the setting in which the data arose. None of these components is sufficient by itself. A technically sophisticated model can answer the wrong question; a sound statistical method can fail when implemented incorrectly; and efficient code cannot repair measurements that do not represent the phenomenon of interest.
Bin Yu’s \(SDC^3\) formulation captures this interdisciplinary breadth. In her 2014 presidential address to the Institute of Mathematical Statistics, she summarized the field as follows (Yu, 2014):
\[
\text{Data science} = S D C^3,
\]
Yu’s notation names five capabilities that need to work together:
Collaboration and communication are not additions made after the technical work is complete. Data-science problems are commonly defined and solved by people with different forms of expertise. Their work becomes useful only when the question, evidence, assumptions, limitations, and conclusions can be understood by others. Data science is therefore both a technical and a social practice.
Consider a study of 311 reports about blocked bicycle lanes. Statistics can help compare report counts across neighborhoods, but domain knowledge is needed to decide whether counts should be divided by lane mileage or another measure of exposure. Computing is needed to combine request records with a map of bicycle lanes. Residents and transportation staff may help explain how reports are made and used. The final analysis must then explain what the counts measure and what they leave out. Each capability answers a different part of the problem.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
Statistics helps us reason from observations while accounting for variation and uncertainty.
Domain knowledge connects an analysis to a question in a particular setting and helps us judge whether its assumptions are sensible.
Computing lets us acquire, organize, explore, and model data.
Collaboration brings together people who understand different parts of a problem, its data, or its methods.
Communication explains the question, evidence, assumptions, and conclusions to people who need to use or evaluate the work.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 The Data-Science Workflow
A data-science project may begin with a problem, an available dataset, or both. Yu and Barter likewise describe a nonlinear data-science life cycle spanning problem formulation, data collection and preparation, analysis, evaluation, and communication (Yu & Barter, 2024). The workflow below adapts that broad life-cycle view for this course and brings questions and evidence into alignment through six recurring activities:

Connect the domain, questions, and data. Use domain knowledge to understand the problem, how the data arose, what the variables measure, and whom the observations represent. Formulate questions the available evidence can address, and obtain additional data when necessary.
Prepare the data. Correct structural problems, handle missing values, combine sources, and record every transformation.
Explore. Use summaries and visualizations to discover patterns, check assumptions, and refine the question.
Model or quantify. Apply methods appropriate to the question and the way the data were collected.
Evaluate. Check statistical, computational, and contextual validity; investigate alternative explanations; and describe uncertainty.
Communicate and act. Present the evidence and its limitations in a form that supports an informed decision.

These activities form a cycle rather than a one-way pipeline. Exploration may reveal a measurement problem, model checking may require different data, and discussion with a domain expert may change the original question. Reproducible records of the data, code, environment, and decisions make such revisions manageable and allow other people to inspect the work.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 This Book’s Emphasis
This book develops practical skills for carrying out and explaining a data-science project. It draws on the nonlinear life-cycle perspective in Yu and Barter’s Veridical Data Science, which develops the PCS framework through case studies (Yu & Barter, 2024). The book takes a different route for beginning students:

The opening chapters build foundations in computing, Git, Quarto, and Python.
The later chapters use a sustained example based on New York City 311 records.
The analysis moves from formulating a question through preparation, exploration, visualization, and modeling to ethical review.

The goal is to connect hands-on implementation with careful checks on what records measure and with conclusions that fit the available evidence.

title: 1  Introduction
1  Introduction
text:
1.5 Computing Foundations
Data science takes place in a computing environment: an operating system, a file system, a command-line shell, a Python installation, project-specific packages, and an editor or notebook interface. These components affect one another. A program that works in one environment may fail in another because a file is in a different location, a package version has changed, or a command is interpreted by a different shell. Understanding the environment is part of reproducible analysis.

1.5.1 Operating Systems and Software
Linux, macOS, and Windows all support data-science work but manage software differently. Installation instructions must therefore be read with the operating system in mind. Linux distributions commonly use system package managers such as APT or DNF; Homebrew is a widely used third-party package manager on macOS; and Windows provides tools such as Windows Package Manager as well as the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL).
An operating-system package manager and a Python package manager solve different problems. The former installs software for the operating system; the latter installs Python libraries into a Python environment. Mixing their roles without understanding which interpreter or environment is active is a common source of installation errors. For course work, use the documented project environment instead of installing packages into an unspecified global Python installation.


1.5.2 Files, Paths, and Directories
A file system organizes files into directories, also called folders. File Explorer on Windows, Finder on macOS, and a command-line shell are different ways of viewing and working with the same file system. A file downloaded in a web browser is not stored “in the browser”: it is saved somewhere in the file system.

1.5.2.1 Finding Your Files
The home directory is the starting point for locating a user’s files. It contains familiar folders such as Desktop, Documents, and usually Downloads. A web browser normally saves a download in Downloads unless the user or browser chooses another location. To find a recent download:

Open the browser’s downloads list and use Show in folder, or open Downloads in File Explorer or Finder.
Check the file name and extension. A file called survey.csv is different from survey.csv.zip or survey (1).csv.
Move course materials from Downloads into a deliberately named project folder. Do not let Downloads become the permanent organization for an analysis.
If the download is a .zip archive, extract it and identify the new folder before trying to run or edit its contents.

From a Unix-like shell, ~ denotes the home directory. The following commands answer three basic questions:
pwd             # Where am I now?
ls              # What is here?
cd ~/Downloads  # Move to my Downloads folder.
The graphical and command-line views should lead to the same location. Run pwd again after cd and compare its output with the location shown in File Explorer or Finder. Software Carpentry provides a guided introduction to this navigation process (Software Carpentry, n.d.).


1.5.2.2 Absolute and Relative Paths
A path identifies a location in the file-system hierarchy. An absolute path starts at the file-system root and identifies a location without reference to the current working directory. Examples include /home/lee/air-quality/data/raw.csv on Linux and C:\Users\Lee\air-quality\data\raw.csv on Windows. Such a path is tied to a particular machine and user account.
A relative path is interpreted from the current working directory. If the working directory is the project folder air-quality, then data/raw.csv identifies the same file without recording where the project is stored. The special path . denotes the current directory and .. denotes its parent. Software Carpentry provides diagrams and exercises for learning how absolute and relative paths are resolved (Software Carpentry, n.d.).
For files within a project, prefer paths relative to the project root. If the whole project directory is moved to a different computer, every internal relative path can remain valid; absolute paths containing a user’s home directory generally cannot. This is why project-relative paths are important for portability and reproducibility. Keep each project in its own directory, separate source data from generated results, and run the analysis with a known project root (Wilson et al., 2017).


1.5.2.3 Naming Files and Folders
Good file and folder names are readable by people and predictable for software. Follow these conventions:

use short, descriptive names such as survey-responses.csv and clean-data.py;
use lowercase letters, digits, hyphens, and underscores, and avoid spaces and characters that have special meanings in a shell;
choose one delimiter convention and apply it consistently;
write dates in sortable YYYY-MM-DD order and zero-pad sequence numbers when ordering matters; and
use stable content-based names instead of names such as final-v2-revised; let version control record revisions.

The Windows directory C:\Program Files illustrates an unfortunate naming convention for command-line work. The space is legal, but a shell may interpret it as the boundary between two arguments unless the entire path is quoted, as in "C:\Program Files". Users must accommodate system paths they do not control, but should not copy this convention into data-science projects. Prefer air-quality to Air Quality Project. Software Carpentry gives the same recommendation because spaces and other shell-sensitive characters complicate commands, loops, and scripts (Software Carpentry, n.d.).
Portable file handling requires attention to case, extensions, and hidden files. Names may be case-sensitive on one operating system but not another, and extensions such as .csv, .py, and .qmd signal different kinds of content. Hidden files often store configuration.
Every file operation should begin with a check of its source and destination. Before reading or writing a file, know the current working directory, the intended path, and whether the operation will replace an existing file.



1.5.3 The Command Line
This book standardizes on Unix shell conventions for command-line work. Its basic commands work in Git Bash, Cygwin, WSL, macOS terminals, and Linux terminals. On Windows, use Git Bash, which is distributed with Git for Windows and provides a Bash emulation for running Git and Unix-style commands (Git for Windows, n.d.).
Do not use PowerShell for the command-line examples in this book. PowerShell defines familiar names such as ls, cp, and rm as aliases for PowerShell cmdlets rather than the corresponding Unix programs. The names may appear to work while their options and behavior differ (Microsoft, n.d.). In this course, use PowerShell only when a Windows-specific software installation step explicitly requires it.
The following shell commands form a useful starting vocabulary:

pwd prints the current working directory;
ls lists directory contents;
cd changes the current directory, with .. denoting its parent;
mkdir creates a directory;
cp copies files or directories;
mv moves or renames files or directories; and
rm removes files.

Options modify the behavior of a command. For example, ls -a includes hidden entries and ls -l displays additional details. Consult a command’s documentation before using unfamiliar options. Use tab completion while typing commands and paths: it completes valid names, reveals what is available, speeds up repetitive work, and reduces errors caused by misspelling or misquoting a file name.
Commands that overwrite or remove data require special care. Check every path before running them; command-line deletion may not use a desktop trash folder.
A short command list is only a starting point for shell fluency. The Software Carpentry lesson The Unix Shell provides a fuller introduction to navigating and modifying files, combining commands with pipes, automating repetition with loops, and writing shell scripts (Software Carpentry, n.d.).


1.5.4 Python and Its Environment
Python is the primary programming language used in this book. A working setup requires a supported Python 3 interpreter, an isolated environment containing the required packages, and an interface for editing and running code. The interface may be a notebook, an editor, or an integrated development environment; the underlying project should remain reproducible regardless of which interface is used.
Readable code is easier to verify, revise, and share. Python’s principal style guide is PEP 8 (Van Rossum et al., 2001). For a start, follow three conventions:

use four spaces for each indentation level and do not mix tabs and spaces;
give variables and functions descriptive lower_case_with_underscores names; and
use whitespace consistently, keep statements on separate lines, and wrap long lines inside parentheses when they become difficult to read.

Consistent style makes analytical code easier to inspect and trust. Clear code exposes assumptions and makes errors easier to find, but consistency within a project matters more than mechanically applying a rule that reduces readability.
Two freely available books provide broader instruction in the Python data-science ecosystem. The Python Data Science Handbook (VanderPlas, 2016) covers NumPy, pandas, visualization, and machine learning, while Python for Data Analysis (McKinney, 2022) develops data manipulation with pandas in greater depth.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.6 Tools for Reproducible Data Science
Coursework should produce artifacts that remain useful after the semester ends. When an assignment is written in Quarto, its clear prose, executable analysis, figures, citations, and reproducible source can be revised into a research memo, portfolio sample, lab report, or presentation for another audience. Students should therefore treat homework as practice for professional communication, not as a disposable file submitted only for a grade; attractive output is valuable because it helps readers understand trustworthy work, not because appearance can substitute for sound reasoning (Quarto Developers, 2025).

1.6.1 Installing Quarto
Quarto is the publishing tool used throughout this book, so install it before you try to render a .qmd file. Follow the official Quarto installation guide for your operating system, then verify the installation from Git Bash, WSL, macOS Terminal, or a Linux shell:
quarto --version
quarto check
The quarto command must be available on your PATH. If the shell reports command not found, finish the installation or reopen the shell so it reloads the updated PATH. Chapter 3 combines Quarto with Python and Jupyter to produce executable documents (Quarto Developers, 2025).
You can test the installation with a minimal document before working on the book. Create hello.qmd with the following contents:
---
title: "Hello, Quarto"
format: html
---

# A Short Introduction

This document was rendered by **Quarto**.

## What I Am Learning

I am practicing Markdown before adding executable analysis.

- headings organize a document;
- emphasis draws attention to important words; and
- links connect the document to [Quarto's guide](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/).
From the directory containing the file, run:
quarto render hello.qmd
Quarto should create hello.html. Open that file in a browser and check that the title and sentence appear. The source file is the record of what you wrote; the HTML file is generated output and should not replace the source.


1.6.2 Installing Git
Git is the version-control tool used throughout this book, so install it before you begin the collaboration exercises. Follow the official Git installation instructions, or install Git for Windows and use Git Bash on Windows. Verify the installation and identity from your shell:
git --version
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --list --show-origin
Chapter 2 explains repositories, commits, branches, remotes, and pull requests. This chapter only asks you to install and verify Git; do not install project packages globally.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.7 Responsible Practice
Ethical questions occur throughout a project, not only when results are published. Data may have been collected without meaningful consent, omit groups affected by a decision, encode historical inequities, or reveal private information when combined with other sources. A model may distribute errors unevenly, and a technically correct analysis may still be used for a harmful or unjustified purpose.
Responsible practice starts with questions about the data and the decisions they may inform:

Who created the data, and who is represented or missing?
Who may benefit from the analysis, and who may bear its risks?
What information is necessary to collect and retain?
How will sensitive information be protected, and how will the data source and transformations be documented?
Could results or model errors differ across relevant groups?
What limitations should readers know before acting on a result?

Legal compliance is necessary in regulated settings, but it does not replace ethical judgment. A dataset can be public and still raise questions about privacy, coverage, or how its results will be used.
Accountability remains with the people conducting and deploying an analysis. This is especially important when AI generates code, models, or prose. The apparent fluency of an output is not evidence that the data were appropriate, the computation was correct, or the conclusion was justified. Every result must be examined with the same statistical, computational, contextual, and ethical scrutiny regardless of how it was produced.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.8 Communicating Data Science
An analysis is useful when its audience can understand what was learned and decide how to respond. A clear explanation usually answers four questions:

What question did the analysis address?
What did the data show?
What evidence supports that finding?
What can and cannot be concluded from it?

Tables and graphics should have a clear purpose, informative labels, honest scales, and enough context to be interpreted without guesswork. For example, a chart titled “Illegal parking increased” makes a stronger claim than a chart titled “311 illegal-parking requests by day.” The first suggests a change in actual violations; the second states what was counted.
Good communication also makes uncertainty and limitations visible. Report what the data cover, distinguish observed patterns from explanations, and avoid causal language when the design supports only association. Provide enough information about data sources, software, and analytical choices for others to inspect or reproduce the work. The objective is not to make a result sound certain; it is to make the reasoning transparent and useful. ## Exercises {.unnumbered}
Write one .qmd file containing your answers to all problems.

 1.1 Prepare your computer for this course.

Install Git and Quarto, record your operating system and the outputs of git --version, quarto --version, and quarto check, and configure and verify your Git identity.
Explain one installation problem and its solution.
State which commands you used to verify both installations.



 1.2 Find and describe a file without relying on a graphical application’s recent- files list.

Use pwd, ls, and cd to locate your home directory and Downloads.
Describe that folder with both an absolute path and a path relative to your project directory, and explain why the relative path is more portable.
Explain why the relative path is preferable when the project is moved to another computer.



 1.3 Establish naming and organization conventions for a new project.

Create a practice directory containing three files with recommended names and one deliberately difficult name.
Explain why the difficult name causes trouble in a shell, rename it, and show the commands and directory listing.
Why do professionals use the command line for project work?
Why do Linux and Windows organize software differently?
Why should source files be separated from generated or binary files?
Give one collaboration problem caused by spaces in names, lines longer than 80 characters, or untracked output.

title: 2  Project Management
text:
2.1 The Git Model
Git records the history of a project so that an analyst can work reproducibly, recover from mistakes, and collaborate without exchanging unnamed copies of files. GitHub and similar services host Git repositories online; they add backup, discussion, and review around Git’s local history. This chapter introduces the ideas and commands needed for the projects in this book. The free Pro Git book provides a fuller reference (Chacon & Straub, 2014).
Several resources provide additional ways to practice:
These resources also introduce ideas used by other version-control systems: keeping a history, recovering earlier work, and coordinating contributions. As you practice, check the result of a command with git status and read the repository’s instructions before changing its files.
GitHub is one hosting service for Git repositories; Bitbucket and GitLab offer similar services. Hosting a repository online provides a backup of committed work and makes collaboration with classmates and coworkers easier.
A Git repository is a project directory together with a database of its history. The working tree contains files being edited, the staging area records changes intended for the next snapshot, and a commit stores that snapshot with an author, time, and message. Thinking in these three states prevents the common mistake of treating git add as a backup or git commit as an upload.
The staging area lets you choose exactly what enters the next commit. Suppose you edit a chapter and also download a large dataset for local analysis. You can stage the chapter alone, inspect it, and commit that coherent change while leaving the dataset out. A commit message should state the change in the imperative mood, such as content: clarify relative paths. Generated files, credentials, and large local data should not be committed.

title: 2  Project Management
text:
2.2 Installing and Configuring Git
Install Git before creating a repository. Use Git for Windows on Windows, and use the package manager or installer appropriate for macOS or Linux; the official Git downloads page lists current options (Git Project, 2025). On Windows, open Git Bash for the Unix-style commands used in this book.
Git needs an identity so that each commit records who made it, and a remote account provides a place to share those commits. Set your local name and email once on a computer, then verify the values:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --list --show-origin
An account on GitHub is separate from a local Git installation. Set up GitHub by creating an account, generating an SSH key if you do not already have one, and adding the key’s public half to your GitHub account; HTTPS authentication is an alternative. GitHub’s onboarding guide explains account setup and authentication (GitHub, 2025b).

title: 2  Project Management
text:
2.3 A First Local Workflow
The safest beginner workflow is to inspect, stage, inspect again, and then commit. Start by cloning an existing repository or initializing a new one:
git clone https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY.git
cd REPOSITORY

# For a new local project instead:
git init
The git status command is the most useful diagnostic tool. It reports the current branch, changed files, staged files, and files Git is ignoring. Run it before and after each logical operation rather than guessing what Git will do. The following sequence records a small change:
git status
git diff                 # changes not yet staged
git add path/to/file.qmd
git diff --staged        # changes that will enter the commit
git commit -m "content: explain the Git workflow"
git status
These commands have separate effects:

git add places selected changes in the staging area. It does not upload them.
git commit saves a snapshot of staged changes in the local repository. It does not publish them.
git push sends local commits to a remote repository, such as GitHub.

After git add, use git diff --staged to check what the next commit will contain. After git commit, use git status to check whether anything remains uncommitted. This sequence helps distinguish saved local work from work that has been shared or backed up remotely.
Beginners should avoid git add . because it stages every unignored change below the current directory, including files they may not have inspected or intended to commit. Stage named files, such as git add 02-git.qmd, and review git diff --staged before committing. Use git add . only when you have deliberately checked every change in the directory.
The commands used most often in this book are:

git clone copies a remote repository to your computer.
git pull downloads and integrates updates from a remote.
git status shows changed, staged, and untracked files and whether the local branch is ahead of or behind its remote.
git add stages selected changes; git rm removes a file from the index and working tree.
git commit records a local snapshot with a message.
git push sends local commits to a remote repository.

The commands git diff and git branch help review changes and manage lines of work. Use git reset only after learning how it changes the branch and staging area.

title: 2  Project Management
text:
2.4 Inspecting and Recovering History
Git’s history commands let you understand a change before trying to undo it. Use a compact log for the sequence of commits and a diff for exact lines:
git log --oneline --decorate --graph --all
git show COMMIT
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD
Different recovery commands have different safety implications. For example, git restore path/to/file discards unstaged edits, git restore --staged path/to/file unstages a file without changing its contents, and git revert COMMIT creates a new commit that reverses an earlier published commit. Avoid git reset on a shared branch until you understand how it changes history.

title: 2  Project Management
text:
2.5 Branches and Remotes
A branch is a movable name for a line of commits. Branches let you develop and review an idea without changing the shared default branch:
git switch -c improve-introduction
# edit files, then add and commit
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
git switch improve-introduction
A remote is a name for another repository, usually an online copy called origin. These commands inspect and synchronize it:
git remote -v
git fetch origin
git pull --ff-only origin main
git push -u origin improve-introduction
The git fetch command downloads remote history without changing working files; git pull fetches and then integrates the selected branch. Pull before starting work when others may have pushed changes, and push completed commits so that a second copy exists.
Git reports a conflict when two changes cannot be integrated automatically. Use this sequence to resolve one:
git status                         # list conflicted files
# open each conflicted file and choose the intended content
# remove the <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers
git add path/to/resolved-file.qmd
git diff --staged                  # inspect the resolution
git commit                         # finish the merge, if Git requests it
Do not choose a side blindly. Ask the contributor who made the other change when the intended result is unclear, and run the project’s checks after the resolution. If you need to abandon an unfinished merge, use git merge --abort before making further edits.

title: 2  Project Management
text:
2.6 GitHub and Pull Requests
GitHub is a hosting and collaboration service, not a replacement for Git. A repository on GitHub can store the canonical source, while each contributor works in a local clone and exchanges commits through a remote.
A pull request proposes merging a branch into another branch. It gives reviewers a place to inspect the diff, discuss design and evidence, and run checks before the change is merged.
Small pull requests are easier to review and less likely to conceal an accidental change. Include the motivation, files affected, and checks you ran; do not include rendered _book/ output when it is generated by the project.
GitHub’s pull-request process is easiest to follow as a sequence of checks:

Fork the upstream repository and synchronize the fork if it is out of date.
Clone your fork and confirm that you can open the project in your editor.
Run git status to verify that the working tree is clean.
Create a descriptive branch, make the change, and run the relevant checks.
Run git status and inspect the diff before staging and committing.
Push the branch, open the pull request, and describe the change for reviewers.

GitHub provides a short pull requests in 100 seconds video, and its documentation explains the full workflow (GitHub, 2025a).
For a class-notes contribution, the concrete command-line sequence looks like this:
git clone https://github.com/GitHub_Username/ids-book.git
cd ids-book
git status
git switch -c branch-name
# edit a file, for example index.qmd, and save it
git status
git add index.qmd
git diff --staged
git commit -m "content: add a useful example"
git push -u origin branch-name
Replace GitHub_Username and branch-name with your own values. On GitHub, open the fork, click Compare & pull request, describe the change, and click Create pull request. If you are on the wrong branch, use git switch existing-branch; use git branch to list branches and identify the current one. Before beginning work, use Sync fork on GitHub when the fork is behind the upstream repository.

title: 2  Project Management
text:
2.7 Practical Recommendations
The following checklist turns the chapter’s concepts into everyday repository habits:

Use the command-line interface instead of the web interface for Git operations, such as uploading files to GitHub.
Make frequent small commits instead of rare large commits.
Make commit messages informative and meaningful.
Name files and folders with lowercase letters and no spaces.
Keep the repository clean by not tracking generated files.
Create and maintain a .gitignore file for generated output, caches, local environments, and secrets.
Keep source lines under 80 characters so that diffs remain readable.
Run git status before and after important operations.
Inspect a diff before staging and inspect the staged diff before committing.
Pull before starting work when collaborators may have pushed changes, and push completed commits so that a second copy exists.

Git tracks text changes well but is not a data warehouse. Keep reproducible scripts, small instructional data, and environment specifications under version control; keep credentials, huge raw datasets, and generated results out of the repository. Record where excluded data came from and how to obtain it so another analyst can reproduce the work.
Use this file-level rule when deciding what belongs in a repository:

Track: source code (.py, .qmd, and .R), documentation, small example data, configuration needed to reproduce the project, environment specifications, and .gitignore.
Do not track: passwords, API keys, private keys, personal data, huge raw datasets, downloaded installers, temporary files, caches, virtual environments, rendered _book/ output, or other files generated from the tracked source.

Put the exclusion rule in .gitignore before creating files that should not be tracked. If sensitive information is accidentally committed, deleting the file in a later commit does not remove it from the earlier history; change the exposed credential and seek help to remove the history safely. ## Exercises {.unnumbered}
Write one .qmd file containing your answers to all problems.

 2.1 Establish a local working copy of the course class-notes repository. For Fall 2026, use statds/ids-f26.

Create a GitHub account if necessary and configure SSH authentication, or explain why you selected HTTPS.

Configure your Git name and email, then use git remote -v, git branch --show-current, and git status to inspect the clone.
Explain the difference between your fork, your local clone, and the remote named origin. Record any obstacle and how you resolved it.



 2.2 Practice a safe local Git workflow before editing the class notes.

Update the default branch with git pull --ff-only, then create and switch to a descriptive branch.
Create a small text file with a lowercase name and make a deliberate change to it. Inspect git status and git diff before staging anything.
Stage the named file, inspect git diff --staged, and make one coherent commit with an informative imperative message.
Use git log --oneline and git show to inspect the commit you made.
Explain why git add . is risky for beginners and why a commit is not the same as a push.



 2.3 Add your wishlist contribution to the class notes.

Locate the wishlist in the class-notes repository and preserve its existing Markdown structure and alphabetical order.
Add your name and two or three goals as a nested Markdown list. Use a lowercase, space-free filename for any additional file you create.
Inspect the change with git diff, stage only the intended source file, and inspect git diff --staged before committing.
Make at least ten small, meaningful commits for this contribution, using informative messages and keeping each commit understandable on its own.
Use git status and git log --oneline to verify that the branch contains the intended history and no generated files or credentials. In your .qmd, record the branch name, the commit hashes and messages, and the relevant command output or a concise summary of it.
Explain why the wishlist belongs in the text source but a rendered HTML file, virtual environment, or cache does not belong in the repository.



 2.4 Share the wishlist contribution for review.

Push your branch to your fork and open a pull request against the course class-notes repository. In your .qmd, give the fork and pull-request links, branch name, latest commit hash, and a one-paragraph description of the proposed change.
Describe the purpose of the change, the files it affects, and the checks you ran so a reviewer can understand the proposal; include the commands and concise results, not an unfiltered terminal transcript.
Respond to a review comment with a focused follow-up commit, then inspect the updated diff.
If the branch cannot be merged cleanly, identify the conflict markers, choose the intended content with the other contributor, stage the resolved file, and complete the merge or rebase safely.

title: 3  Reproducible Data Science
text:
3.1 A Minimal Quarto Document
Quarto turns plain-text source into reproducible documents that combine explanation, computation, results, figures, and references. A data-science analysis should be reproducible because readers need to inspect how evidence was produced, not merely see a final picture or a pasted table. Quarto supports Python, R, Julia, and Observable and can publish articles, reports, websites, books, and presentations in several output formats (Quarto Developers, 2025b).
This chapter is a jump start, not a replacement for the complete Quarto Guide. Use the guide when you need options not covered here, and consult the Python documentation, Markdown reference, and presentation documentation for detailed examples (Quarto Developers, 2025d, 2025a, 2025c).
A Quarto document is a text file whose .qmd extension combines YAML metadata, Markdown prose, equations, citations, and executable code chunks. The following small document is a better starting point than a code-only hello-world: it produces a numerical result, a table, and a figure from the same code that explains them.
Create a file named hello.qmd with YAML metadata like this:
The document can then combine prose, equations, and executable code. Equation punctuation follows ordinary sentence punctuation. The mean of observations \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) is given by Equation 3.1.
The source syntax for this numbered equation is:
\[
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i.
\tag{3.1}\]
A cases display can continue a sentence with a comma, as shown in Equation 3.2:
\[
g(x) =
\begin{cases}
  0, & x < 0,\\
  1, & x \ge 0.
\end{cases}
\tag{3.2}\]
The comma after the first case and the period after the final case are part of one grammatical statement. The code below generates a table and a figure from the same observations:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from matplotlib_inline.backend_inline import set_matplotlib_formats

set_matplotlib_formats("svg")

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
scores = pd.DataFrame(
    rng.normal(loc=[78, 72, 84], scale=[9, 8, 7], size=(30, 3)).round(1),
    columns=["data science", "statistics", "programming"],
    index=range(1, 31),
)
scores.index.name = "student"
scores.head()

mean_scores = scores.mean()
standard_errors = scores.sem()
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(mean_scores.index, mean_scores, yerr=standard_errors, capsize=4)
ax.set(xlabel="Subject", ylabel="Mean score", title="Simulated class scores")
plt.show()







Figure 3.1: Mean simulated score by subject for a class of 30 students; error bars show standard errors
The call to default_rng(2026) creates a seeded random-number generator. The same seed reproduces the same simulated scores when the document is rendered again. The loc values set the three subjects’ generating means, while the scale values set their standard deviations. In the figure:
The error bars do not show the range of student scores. For that question, we would also display the individual scores or a distribution plot. This distinction helps readers avoid treating a summary figure as if it showed every observation. Quarto itself is documented in the Quarto Guide (Quarto Developers, 2025b).
The opening and closing lines between --- define YAML metadata. Headings use one or more # characters, ordinary text forms paragraphs, dollar signs mark LaTeX equations, and a fenced code chunk begins with ```{python}. The jupyter: python3 setting tells Quarto which Jupyter kernel should execute Python chunks. Expressions whose values are displayed, such as scores, and figures returned by the chunk become part of the rendered document.
Render the document from its directory:
Quarto writes hello.html by default. Open that file in a browser, or use quarto preview hello.qmd while editing to render again after each save. Keep the .qmd source under version control; treat the rendered HTML as generated output.

$$

title: 3  Reproducible Data Science
text:
3.2 Markdown Essentials
Markdown provides the readable structure around an analysis. The following mini-report shows how headings, emphasis, a list, a labeled equation, a table, a figure, a citation, and cross-references work together:
## Assessment Results {#sec-assessment-results}

The **mean score** summarizes performance in each subject, but it does not show
the variation among students. The sample mean for subject $s$ is

$$
\bar{x}_s = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{is}.
$$ {#eq-subject-mean}

@tbl-subject-means reports the results calculated with
@eq-subject-mean.

| subject | mean score |
|:--|--:|
| data science | 78.4 |
| statistics | 72.1 |
| programming | 84.3 |

: Simulated mean scores for a class of 30 students. {#tbl-subject-means}

![Mean score by subject, with standard-error bars.](figures/scores.svg){#fig-subject-means}

@fig-subject-means makes the difference among simulated subject means easier
to compare. The bars do not show how individual students performed. The
standard-error bars describe uncertainty in the estimated means, while a
spread plot would be needed to compare variation among students. This is why
the figure caption names the quantity represented by the bars and intervals.
A label in braces, such as {#eq-subject-mean}, identifies an object that Quarto should number. Use the prefixes eq-, tbl-, fig-, and sec- for equations, tables, figures, and sections. A cross-reference begins with @ and uses the matching label, as in @tbl-subject-means. During rendering, Quarto replaces that source text with the current object number. If an earlier table or figure is added, references update automatically instead of leaving a stale number in the prose.
Use a heading hierarchy rather than bold text to organize a document. Put blank lines around paragraphs, tables, and lists; write descriptive link text; and keep executable code in a Quarto code chunk. For each figure or table, a caption should identify its subject and any key qualifications. For example, “Mean score by subject, with standard-error bars” tells readers more than “Results.” Cite sources near the claims they support. The Markdown basics reference covers tables, images, citations, cross-references, callouts, and other features.

title: 3  Reproducible Data Science
text:
3.3 Why the Software Environment Matters
An analysis is a combination of source code and the software environment that interprets it. Two computers can run the same source and obtain different results when they use different Python versions, package versions, operating- system libraries, or default settings. A result that cannot be rerun after an environment changes is not fully reproducible, even when the code is available (Wilson et al., 2017).
An isolated environment makes these dependencies explicit and prevents one project from silently changing another. Recording the Python version and the installed packages lets a collaborator recreate the computational setting, while a lockfile or pinned requirements file records the versions tested here. This practice also makes failures diagnosable: when an upgrade changes an output, we can identify the change instead of guessing which global installation caused it.

title: 3  Reproducible Data Science
text:
3.4 Python Environments for Quarto
Quarto executes Python through a Jupyter kernel, so the interpreter and packages must be installed in an environment that Quarto can find. A virtual environment keeps this project’s packages separate from the system Python and from unrelated projects.
This book uses Python 3.12 in its tested environment. You may choose a virtual environment’s name and location. A virtual environment is a directory containing an isolated Python installation and its packages; it does not contain a project’s source files or build instructions. The uv command-line tool installs Python versions, creates virtual environments, and installs packages; it is not a replacement for Python or Quarto.
uv venv --python 3.12 /path/to/your/environment
source /path/to/your/environment/bin/activate
If uv is unavailable, replace uv venv with python3.12 -m venv and use the same path. Do not install packages into the system Python, and do not commit a virtual-environment directory. Keep the project’s environment specification and source files under version control instead.
Use python --version, which python, and jupyter kernelspec list to verify that the active interpreter is Python 3.12 and is the one you intend to use. If Quarto reports that it cannot find a kernel, select the environment’s Python interpreter in your editor or install its kernel with python -m ipykernel install --user.

title: 3  Reproducible Data Science
text:
3.5 Reproducibility in Practice
Reproducibility requires a record of the inputs, environment, instructions, and decisions that produced an analysis. A Quarto file brings prose and executable code together, but it cannot by itself make an undocumented dataset, unrecorded random seed, or unavailable package reproducible.
For each analysis, preserve these five components:

Source: the .qmd file and any scripts it calls.
Data: the source, version, download date, and transformations for each dataset; keep private or large raw data outside Git when necessary.
Environment: the Python version, package requirements, Quarto version, and operating-system details needed to run the source.
Execution: the commands, options, random seeds, and order of steps used to render the document.
Outputs: tables, figures, and conclusions checked against the source, not manually edited after rendering.

Use relative project paths, pin important package versions, set random seeds when simulation is involved, and render from a clean working tree. These habits make it possible for another analyst to inspect and repeat the work (Wilson et al., 2017).

title: 3  Reproducible Data Science
text:
3.6 Rendering the Book
Rendering the notes locally lets you see how the published book is produced, practice the workflow used in a shared data-science project, and test a correction or improvement before proposing it in a pull request. A successful render shows that the source, computations, citations, and cross-references work together on your computer. To obtain a local copy, clone the repository and enter it:
git clone https://github.com/statds/ids-book.git
cd ids-book
Assume that you have already activated a Python 3.12 environment as described in Section 3.4. The cloned repository contains the Makefile. From its root, install this book’s pinned dependencies and build it:
make install
make check
make render
If you want an environment dedicated to this book, choose a directory for it, create it, and activate it before running those commands. For example, replace /path/to/ids-book-env below with a directory of your choice:
uv venv --python 3.12 /path/to/ids-book-env
source /path/to/ids-book-env/bin/activate
If uv is unavailable, replace uv venv with python3.12 -m venv and use the same path. Activation sets VIRTUAL_ENV, which this repository’s Makefile uses to select Python. The make install target installs the pinned packages from requirements.txt; make check verifies the command-line tools; and make render builds the complete book in _book/. Open _book/index.html in a browser to inspect that completed build. While actively editing the book, make preview starts a local server and rebuilds the output when source files change. Students building the book should not run make req, because that maintainer target rewrites requirements.txt from the local environment.
Read the repository’s Makefile rather than treating its commands as magic. It is a short, plain-text description of the build tasks. Use an AI assistant to ask what a specific target, variable, or command does, then compare the answer with the Makefile and test it with a command such as make -n render, which prints the commands without running them. This is a useful way to learn an unfamiliar project while retaining responsibility for checking the explanation. For a quick test of one source file, use:
make render-one FILE=hello.qmd
Read the terminal output rather than assuming a successful command produced a correct document. Check that code results make sense, links work, figures have captions, citations resolve, and the output contains no accidental secrets or local file paths. Generated _book/, .quarto/, and cache files belong in .gitignore, not in a commit.

title: 3  Reproducible Data Science
text:
3.7 Presentations with Quarto
Quarto can turn a .qmd file into a presentation as well as a report. The same source can be adapted for different audiences while keeping the analysis available for review. For example, a homework report might include code and diagnostics, while a presentation might show only the question, main result, and limitations. The presentation guide describes the available formats (Quarto Developers, 2025b).
For a data-science assignment, keep the source record in text files:

the .qmd file contains the explanation, code, citations, and references;
separate scripts hold reusable computations;
data documentation records sources, dates, and transformations; and
an environment specification records software dependencies.

The rendered HTML or PDF is an output for readers. Word-processing and slide files can be useful for delivery, but they do not show the line-by-line source history or reliably record how a manually edited result was computed. Git preserves revisions, and executable code keeps tables and figures linked to their data (Wilson et al., 2017).
Create a presentation by choosing a presentation format in the YAML header:
---
title: "A Data-Science Result"
format: revealjs
---

## The Question

What decision does this analysis support?

## The Evidence

Explain the important figure and its limitations.
Render it with quarto render presentation.qmd or preview it with quarto preview presentation.qmd. Use headings for slides, keep one central idea on each slide, and write speaker notes when additional explanation belongs in the oral presentation rather than on the slide. Export a PDF only when a course or audience requires a static copy; keep the .qmd source as the authoritative presentation. ## Exercises {.unnumbered}
Complete the Git setup in Section 1.6.2 and the Quarto installation in Section 1.6.1 before beginning. Write one .qmd file containing your answers to all problems.

 3.1 Follow the complete workflow in Section 3.6 to clone and render this book from source. In the assignment .qmd, report the following evidence:

Record the commands and concise results of git remote -v and git status in the cloned repository.
Record the environment path, the command used to create it (or state that you used an existing environment), and the result of python --version.
Record concise results from make install, make check, and make render. Confirm that the rendered home page is _book/index.html, and describe any error you fixed.
Explain why the virtual-environment directory and _book should not be committed, while the source files, requirements.txt, and _quarto.yml should be tracked.



 3.2 Build a small, reproducible analysis in your assignment .qmd. Use the Hello, Quarto Jupyter tutorial as the starting point for its polar-axis figure. Do not create a second document.

Adapt the tutorial’s polar-axis Python code into an executable code chunk, then render the assignment successfully. Give the figure a descriptive caption and label, and refer to it by its automatically generated number in a complete sentence.
Add the displayed equation below using the shown label. In the sentence immediately before or after it, refer to the equation as @eq-polar and explain that it defines the angle used by the Python code.
\[
\theta = 2\pi r, \qquad 0 \le r < 2.
\tag{3.3}\]
From the same r and theta values used for the plot, generate a table of at least five selected pairs. Give the table a caption and label, then refer to it by its automatically generated number in a complete sentence.
Add a BibTeX entry for the Hello, Quarto tutorial to the assignment bibliography, cite it in the prose with its citation key, and verify that the rendered References section contains the entry.
Write two or three complete sentences that interpret the equation, table, and figure together. Include one limitation of this example.
Check that the document has no unresolved citations or cross-references and that its displayed results are generated by the source code. Render the document while saving the messages, then search the log for warnings: quarto render homework.qmd 2>&1 | tee render.log followed by rg -i 'warning|not found|undefined|citation|reference|broken' render.log. Inspect the rendered document for ??, missing labels, and missing bibliography entries. State the checks you performed and any correction you made in the .qmd; do not commit the generated log.



 3.3 Make the document ready for reproducible collaboration.

Identify the source files, data inputs, software environment, commands, and outputs another analyst would need to reproduce the work.
Distinguish files that belong under version control from a virtual environment, cache, generated HTML, or other output that should be ignored.
Explain how relative paths, pinned package versions, and a recorded random seed would help another student obtain the same results.

title: 4  Python Practice
text:
4.1 Python Ecosystem
This chapter develops Python habits that help you inspect and reproduce an analysis. It assumes that you have seen variables, functions, conditionals, and loops. In particular, you will learn to:
These habits help turn a short script into an analysis that another person can inspect and rerun. Each section connects a Python concept to a practical question you may encounter while working with data.
A Python process runs code in one interpreter, which supplies the language and standard library. An environment adds third-party packages such as NumPy and pandas. These related terms describe different layers of the Python ecosystem:
The standard library includes modules such as math, pathlib, and statistics; NumPy and pandas are third-party libraries rather than parts of Python itself (McKinney, 2022; Python Software Foundation, 2026c).
These distinctions help diagnose a common problem: pip reports that a library is installed, but import pandas still fails. The package may have been installed for a different interpreter than the one running the code. The word used to install a distribution can also differ from the import name: the scikit-learn distribution, for example, is imported as sklearn. Check the active interpreter and the exact import name before reinstalling packages.
When code fails with ModuleNotFoundError, first determine which interpreter is active. This chunk reports the interpreter path and version used by the current Quarto document:
import sys

print(sys.executable)
print(sys.version.split()[0])

/home/junyan/work/teaching/ids-book/.ids/bin/python3
3.12.14
In a terminal, python --version and which python provide similar evidence after an environment has been activated. Use python -m pip, rather than a bare pip, to ensure that package management uses that same interpreter:
A virtual environment is a self-contained directory with a chosen Python installation and its packages. It prevents one project’s package version from silently changing another project’s behavior. The exact package versions in requirements.txt are part of a reproducible analysis because another person can install the same set with python -m pip install -r requirements.txt (Python Software Foundation, 2026d; Wilson et al., 2017). Section 3.4 showed how this book uses the .ids environment; the important practice here is to check the interpreter, not merely the command prompt.

title: 4  Python Practice
text:
Interpreter: The program that runs Python code and supplies the standard library.
Module: A unit that Python’s import system loads as a module object. A module can come from a Python source file, a compiled extension, built-in code, or another source.
Package: A special module that can contain submodules. A regular package is commonly a directory with an __init__.py file, while a namespace package can span locations and needs no such file.
Library: An informal term for a reusable body of code and documentation, such as NumPy or pandas.
Distribution: The installable unit managed by tools such as pip. One distribution can provide one or more importable packages or modules.






python -m pip show numpy
python -m pip show pandas
python -m pip freeze

title: 4  Python Practice
text:
4.2 Imports
An import statement binds a name in the current file to a module or an object defined elsewhere. Choose imports that make the source easy to read and avoid names that obscure where a function comes from:

import math
from pathlib import Path

project_root = Path.cwd()
print(math.sqrt(81))
print(project_root.name)

9.0
ids-book


For widely used data-science libraries, conventional aliases make code easier to recognize:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

Avoid from package import *. It hides the source of each name, can overwrite an existing name, and makes a traceback harder to interpret. When you need to learn what an imported object does, use help(), inspect its documentation, or check its type and attributes deliberately:

sample = np.array([2, 4, 8])

print(type(sample))
print(sample.dtype)
print(sample.shape)

<class 'numpy.ndarray'>
int64
(3,)


The type, dtype, and shape attributes answer different questions. The first identifies the Python or library object; dtype describes how an array stores its values; and shape gives its dimensions. Checking all three is often more informative than printing a large object.

title: 4  Python Practice
4  Python Practice
text:
4.4 Names and Objects
Python names refer to objects. Assignment usually binds another name to the same object; it does not copy that object. Every object has an identity, type, and value. Lists and dictionaries are mutable, while numbers, strings, and tuples are immutable (Python Software Foundation, 2026b).

scores = [82, 91, 87]
alias = scores
copy = scores.copy()

alias.append(76)

print(scores)
print(alias is scores)
print(copy)
print(copy is scores)

[82, 91, 87, 76]
True
[82, 91, 87]
False


The call to append changes the list object that both scores and alias refer to. The copy variable refers to a distinct list, so it retains the earlier values. Use is only to ask whether two names refer to the same object; use == to ask whether their values are equal.
This distinction matters at function boundaries. An in-place function has a side effect because it modifies the caller’s list. A function that creates and returns a new list is generally safer for a data-analysis transformation.

def add_bonus_in_place(values: list[float], bonus: float) -> None:
    """Add bonus to each value by changing values itself."""
    for index in range(len(values)):
        values[index] += bonus


def with_bonus(values: list[float], bonus: float) -> list[float]:
    """Return bonus-adjusted values without changing values itself."""
    return [value + bonus for value in values]


original = [82, 91, 87]
adjusted = with_bonus(original, 3)
add_bonus_in_place(original, 3)

print(adjusted)
print(original)

[85, 94, 90]
[85, 94, 90]


Neither style is universally correct. Mutating a large object can be efficient, and some library methods intentionally modify objects in place. The important rule is that a function’s name, docstring, and use should make mutation clear. When in doubt, assign a returned object to a new, descriptive name and retain the original until you have checked the result.

4.5 Data Structures
Lists are flexible containers that can hold objects of different types. NumPy arrays store a regularly shaped collection of values of one dtype, which makes elementwise numerical operations concise. A pandas data frame organizes named columns that can have different types. Select the structure that matches the task, rather than treating them as interchangeable.

values = [1, 2, 3]
array = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
table = pd.DataFrame({"student": ["A", "B", "C"], "score": array})

print(array * 10)
table

The expression array * 10 multiplies every array value. In contrast, values * 10 repeats the list ten times. This is not a minor syntactic detail: it changes the object type and the meaning of the operation. Convert to an array when you need regular numerical computation; use a data frame when the observations have named variables and you need to inspect, join, summarize, or plot columns (McKinney, 2022; VanderPlas, 2016).
NumPy operations are often vectorized: one expression applies the same calculation to every array element without an explicit Python loop. Vectorized operations are usually faster for large regular arrays, while loops remain appropriate for branching logic and one-game simulations (VanderPlas, 2016):

array**2

array([1., 4., 9.])


Python-level loops can be slower for large numerical arrays because Python must interpret each iteration and repeatedly manage dynamically typed objects. A NumPy expression moves the repeated numerical work into compiled code, much as R uses compiled routines behind vectorized operations. When a custom loop cannot be expressed with NumPy or pandas, Python users commonly use [Numba] (https://numba.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user/5minguide.html) to compile suitable numerical functions, or use Cython and compiled extensions for more control. Switching to Julia is another language choice, but it is not required simply because a Python loop is slow.

4.6 Number Representation
Python’s built-in integers grow to represent arbitrarily large whole numbers, subject to available memory. NumPy integers have a fixed width, such as int8 or int64, because fixed-width storage supports compact arrays and fast operations. A value outside that type’s range can overflow:

largest_int8 = np.array([127], dtype=np.int8)
overflowed = largest_int8 + np.array([1], dtype=np.int8)

print(largest_int8.dtype, largest_int8)
print(overflowed)

int8 [127]
[-128]


Inspect dtype before converting identifiers, counts, or monetary values to a small integer type. An overflow may produce a plausible but wrong value, which is more dangerous than a visible error.
Most numerical analysis uses binary floating-point values. Many decimal fractions, including 0.1, have no exact finite binary representation, so a stored float is usually an approximation. This behavior comes from the hardware representation, not from a Python mistake (Python Software Foundation, 2026a). A standard double-precision floating-point value uses a finite sign, exponent, and significand; the Wikipedia article on double-precision floating-point format provides an optional visual explanation of these fields. The limited significand also means that ordinary floating-point values cannot represent every very large integer exactly.

import math

total = 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1
target = 0.3

print(total == target)
print(format(total, ".17f"))
print(math.isclose(total, target))

False
0.30000000000000004
True


Use exact equality for values that are expected to be exactly equal, such as category labels, integer counts, or a known string. For computed floating-point values, use math.isclose or numpy.isclose with tolerances chosen for the scale and purpose of the analysis. Format a final result for readers, but do not mistake rounded display for increased computational accuracy. Use decimal.Decimal when an application requires decimal arithmetic, such as currency calculations with legally defined rounding rules. For calculations that require many decimal digits, set the decimal context inside the function so its result does not depend on hidden notebook state; construct values from exact inputs such as Decimal(1), rather than converting an existing float.

4.7 Simulation
Random simulation is a compact setting in which all of these ideas matter. The Monty Hall game has three doors, one prize, and a host who opens an unchosen empty door. A player who switches wins whenever the first choice was wrong, which has probability two-thirds. The simulation uses a local NumPy random number generator. Supplying the same seed creates the same pseudo-random draws, which makes debugging and review possible.

def simulate_monty_hall(
    n_trials: int, seed: int | None = None
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Estimate stay and switch win rates in the three-door Monty Hall game."""
    if n_trials <= 0:
        raise ValueError("n_trials must be positive")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    prize = rng.integers(0, 3, size=n_trials)
    first_choice = rng.integers(0, 3, size=n_trials)
    stay_wins = (first_choice == prize).sum()
    switch_wins = n_trials - stay_wins
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "strategy": ["stay", "switch"],
        "wins": [stay_wins, switch_wins],
        "win_rate": [stay_wins / n_trials, switch_wins / n_trials],
    })


monty_results = simulate_monty_hall(n_trials=100_000, seed=2026)
monty_results

The function returns a data frame instead of printing a conclusion. That choice lets later code make a table, a figure, or a formal comparison without parsing text. Repeating the call with the same arguments should reproduce the result:

4.8 Debugging
Debugging is the process of finding which assumption in a program failed, not merely making an exception disappear. When a program raises an error or returns an unexpected result, reduce the problem before changing the code. Reproduce it with the smallest input that shows the failure, read the final line of the traceback first, and inspect the smallest object that could explain the behavior.
Python provides several complementary debugging tools. Use type(), repr(), dir(), and help() to inspect ordinary Python objects. Use assert to check program assumptions that should always hold, such as a positive sample size or a matching number of rows. When a program operates on tabular or numerical objects, inspect their types, shapes, missing values, and finite values deliberately:

print(type(monty_results))
print(monty_results.dtypes)
print(monty_results.shape)
print(monty_results.head())
assert monty_results.shape == (2, 3)
assert monty_results["wins"].sum() == 100_000
assert np.isfinite(monty_results["win_rate"]).all()

Pandas supplies additional checks such as .info(), .describe(), .isna(), and .value_counts(). NumPy supplies checks such as .shape, .dtype, np.isnan(), and np.isfinite(). These checks can reveal a wrong column type, unexpected missing values, an empty subset, or a calculation that silently produced infinite values.
For an exception, the traceback module can display the error explicitly in a script. To pause a running program and inspect local variables, insert breakpoint() temporarily or run a script under Python’s standard-library debugger:
python -m pdb analysis.py
In a Jupyter or Quarto notebook, %debug opens the debugger after the most recent exception, and %pdb on enables automatic entry into the debugger after future exceptions. These commands are interactive, so use them while developing rather than in a document that must render unattended.
Turn a successful diagnostic into a repeatable test. A direct assert is often enough for a small function; a test framework such as pytest is useful when a program has many cases. Keep the input small, make the expected result explicit, and test edge cases such as an empty input, a missing value, or a sample size of one.
AI assistants can also help with debugging. Give an assistant the smallest reproducible example, the complete traceback, the relevant function, and the expected behavior. It can explain an unfamiliar message, suggest diagnostic checks, propose a minimal correction, or help write a test. Do not paste credentials, private data, or confidential project code. Treat an AI suggestion as a hypothesis: check it against the official documentation and your source, run the proposed test, and verify that the program now behaves as intended—not only that the exception has disappeared.
Avoid solving an error by repeatedly installing packages, restarting the editor, or changing several unrelated lines at once. Make one hypothesis, test it with a small example, and record the correction in the source or a concise commit message. ## Exercises {.unnumbered}
