title: 5  Problem Formulation
text:
5.1 Introduction
Problem formulation connects a domain purpose, available evidence, and a question the evidence can address. This chapter develops that connection through New York City’s 311 service requests directed to the New York City Police Department (NYPD) during the week containing Labor Day 2026. The available extract is the starting point: its categories and quality checks guide the choice and refinement of an illegal-parking question. Domain context and documentation determine what the resulting analysis can establish.
Before running this chapter’s code, update the local book source and its Python environment so that both match the current version. From the repository directory, pull the latest changes, activate the book’s .ids environment, and install the pinned requirements:
On Windows, activate .ids/Scripts/activate from Git Bash. Keep the environment active while running the chapter’s code.
Problem formulation can begin with a domain problem or an available dataset, but either route must connect a substantive purpose to evidence capable of addressing it. Administrative records are often created to operate a service, then made available for analysis before any research question has been chosen. Their categories, times, locations, and unusual values can suggest questions that an investigator would not have formulated in advance. In this chapter, the NYPD extract’s distribution of reported problems motivates illegal parking as a working topic; a domain purpose and account of what these service requests measure determine whether a resulting question is worth pursuing.
There are two common starting points:
The two routes often meet. A question directs us to inspect particular fields; that inspection may reveal that a field is incomplete or does not measure the concept we need. We may then revise the question, look for another source, or limit the claim. Yu and Barter describe this movement among questions, data, and analysis as a nonlinear data-science life cycle (Yu & Barter, 2024). The 311 extract here was collected to operate a service, not to answer our comparison. A pattern in its records is therefore a starting point for inquiry, not by itself an explanation of parking conditions.
The first activity in the data-science workflow aligns three components:
This alignment gives the \(D\) in the \(SDC^3\) framework a practical role. For the bicycle-lane example, it asks us to check:
Domain knowledge helps answer the first and third questions. Data inspection addresses the second, while statistical reasoning helps with the fourth. Collaboration can reveal assumptions that one analyst might overlook.
A candidate question becomes researchable when its main parts are explicit. For the worked example, they are:
The provisional question is: among NYPD-directed illegal-parking requests from this week, how did recorded closure-time distributions vary across reported problem details? We will revise the question if the detail labels or timestamps do not measure the intended concepts. Because the groups are chosen from the observed records, the comparison is exploratory. Each restriction limits which requests the answer describes and should serve a clear purpose.
Four complementary checks assess whether a candidate question is worth pursuing and whether the available evidence can answer it.
The same checks apply to a study of community risk, but the analysis needs a different unit and evidence. For example, a school-district study should specify:
When counts are small, one additional event can change a rate substantially. An area-level pattern describes areas, not individuals, and does not identify a cause (Openshaw, 1984; Robinson, 1950). Define the event, geographic unit, period, and denominator before assembling the data.
These checks are iterative rather than a one-time screen. A domain concern may lead to a data search, while an observed pattern may suggest a new question; in either direction, checking measurement, scope, and evidence can require revising the question. The sections that follow evaluate the provisional comparison against the downloaded records and refine it in light of what those records can establish.

title: 5  Problem Formulation
text:
Problem to data: A transportation planner asks where blocked bicycle lanes are reported, then looks for records with location and problem fields.
Data to question: An analyst inspects service records and asks which observed pattern might matter to residents or agency staff.




Domain purpose: Why would an answer matter, and who might use it?
Question: What description, comparison, prediction, or decision is sought?
Data: What was observed, how was it measured, and what setting does it represent?



whether the question concerns reports, verified obstructions, or safety;
whether the records identify a location and a report category;
whether the comparison should account for lane length or another exposure;
whether the observations support a description or a stronger claim.




Unit: one NYPD-directed 311 request.
Outcome: the recorded time between request creation and closure.
Place and period: New York City, September 6–12, 2026.
Comparison: closure-time distributions across reported problem details.
Claim: a description of these requests, not all parking conditions.




Domain fit asks whether an answer would inform a substantive concern or decision, and who could use it. A data-first question needs a domain purpose just as a problem-first question needs evidence suited to its purpose.
Measurement fit asks whether the recorded variables represent the concepts in the question. For example, the NYPD records measure time to administrative closure; without further documentation, they do not measure time to an officer’s arrival.
Scope fit asks whether the observational unit, population, place, and period match the intended claim. This extract contains NYPD-directed requests from one week, not every parking condition in New York City.
Evidence fit asks whether the study design supports the proposed descriptive, comparative, predictive, or causal claim. A difference in recorded closure times can describe these requests, but it does not by itself show that problem type caused a difference.



Unit: a district or district-year;
Outcome: a defined event, such as hospitalization or death, with a source suited to that event;
Measure: a count for event burden, or a rate with a stated population denominator; and
Scope: the districts and years the result describes.

title: 5  Problem Formulation
text:
5.2 Interpreting the NYPD 311 Records
The observational unit in this chapter is one New York City 311 service request directed to NYPD. The public dataset records requests routed to responding agencies, and its Unique Key field identifies rows (NYC Open Data, n.d.). A row is neither an independently verified violation nor necessarily a unique street condition: several requests may concern the same situation, while other conditions may never be reported. Request counts therefore measure activity recorded by this service system within a defined scope. A location with few requests may have fewer conditions, less use of 311, or both; the table alone cannot separate those explanations. The identifier must be present and unique if each row is to represent one request in subsequent counts. The downloaded records must also be checked against the stated agency and time restrictions before the illegal-parking problem filter defines the working subset.
The timestamp fields define an administrative interval rather than a direct measure of field response. Created Date records the creation of a request, and Closed Date records its closure by the responding agency; their difference is the recorded closure time. An officer could arrive before that closure, and the reported condition could end at another time. The archive does not contain observations of those events, so relabeling the difference as response or resolution time would change the measured concept without evidence. The timestamps in this extract are local New York clock times without an explicit timezone. The selected week does not cross a daylight-saving transition, which avoids one source of ambiguity in subtracting its recorded times but does not validate each timestamp. An analysis of individual reporting behavior would additionally require information about reporters that the public table does not provide.
Each field has a role in a particular question. For example:

Borough can define broad comparison groups.
Problem Detail (formerly Descriptor) records a reported category.
Unique Key identifies a request; Incident Zip labels a postal area. Keep both as text because their digits are labels, not measured values.
Latitude and longitude locate a recorded point; a police precinct code identifies an administrative area.

These geographic fields can be missing or disagree because they describe different objects. A ZIP label can support an area lookup, but distance to a precinct requires a usable point, a precinct location, and a defined distance measure. Treating these fields as interchangeable would hide which requests can enter the calculation and what each result represents.

title: 5  Problem Formulation
text:
5.3 Acquiring Data
Data acquisition obtains evidence while preserving enough information to interpret and reproduce it. Common sources include local files, public repositories, open-data portals, application programming interfaces (APIs), databases, surveys, experiments, sensors, and administrative systems. The method should match the source and intended use. A stable file is convenient for a fixed classroom or research example, while an API or database query is more appropriate when an analysis must refresh regularly.
A reproducible acquisition records the source and the intended selection rules. The example file came from the NYC Open Data portal, where we attempted to download NYPD requests created during the week containing Labor Day 2026. The portal identifier erm2-nwe9 locates the full 311 dataset and can be used to find its documentation or construct an API request; it is a source identifier, not a request-level key. The archive contains the returned records but not a saved copy of the portal query settings, so the intended filters and the delivered values must be checked separately.
The delivered file does not match the intended time window: it contains 1,902 records created during the first eight hours of September 13. This discrepancy shows why a successful download is not evidence that the portal returned exactly the requested data. The intended agency restriction also requires an independent check against the Agency values in the file.
Raw and derived data serve different purposes. The downloaded source extract preserves what the provider returned. The smaller illegal-parking data frame will be derived in code by applying the intended time restriction and then a problem-category filter while retaining all 44 source columns. Preserving the source makes it possible to audit or revise both filters. The source file should not be edited manually to remove the extra records.
The book distributes the downloaded CSV in a ZIP archive:
data/311_nypd_lbdwk_2026.csv.zip
The archive contains one CSV file and reduces its size by about 90% without changing the tabular source representation. Pandas can decompress a single-member ZIP archive during import. The filename identifies the service, agency, period, and year without depending on spaces or punctuation that require shell quoting. A companion provenance record should carry details that cannot fit sensibly in a filename, including the direct source, access date, requested selection rules, and observed departure from those rules.

5.3.1 Importing the Archive
Reproducible import begins with a project-relative path. A relative path works after another reader clones or moves the project because it describes the file’s location inside the project rather than its location on one person’s computer. The Path class also provides portable operations for checking and measuring the file.

from pathlib import Path
from zipfile import ZipFile

import pandas as pd

data_path = Path("data") / "311_nypd_lbdwk_2026.csv.zip"

if not data_path.exists():
    raise FileNotFoundError(data_path)

with ZipFile(data_path) as archive:
    members = archive.infolist()

if len(members) != 1:
    raise ValueError("The data archive must contain exactly one CSV file.")

csv_member = members[0]

file_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "representation": ["ZIP archive", "Uncompressed CSV"],
    "size_mib": [
        data_path.stat().st_size / 2**20,
        csv_member.file_size / 2**20,
    ],
})
file_summary.round({"size_mib": 2})

identifier_types = {
    "Unique Key": "string",

Instead, they turn assumptions about the extract into results that can be reviewed. The governing principle is to trust the provider while verifying every condition on which the analysis depends.
The first checks address identity, agency, and both temporal boundaries. A portal selection is an instruction about what to return; these checks test whether the delivered records satisfy it. 5.5 Efficient Representation
Data representation affects storage, import time, type preservation, and interoperability. The CSV format is widely supported text that is easy to inspect with ordinary tools. Its simplicity is valuable for acquisition and archival exchange, but each reader must parse the text and reconstruct such types as datetimes and identifiers.
Apache Arrow defines a column-oriented representation designed for efficient analytical data interchange across systems. Feather Version 2 stores Arrow’s interprocess communication format in a portable file and supports typed columns and compression (Apache Arrow Developers, 2026). Bates and Yan describe how an Arrow representation can create a unified dataset for efficient analysis across software platforms (Bates & Yan, 2024).
A derived Feather file can preserve the imported table’s typed representation for repeated analysis. The example writes to a temporary directory so that rendering the chapter does not add a generated file to the project.

from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as temporary_directory:
    feather_path = Path(temporary_directory) / "nypd_download.feather"
    requests.to_feather(feather_path)
    requests_from_feather = pd.read_feather(feather_path)

    representation = pd.DataFrame({
        "format": ["CSV", "ZIP-compressed CSV", "Feather"],
        "size_mib": [
            csv_member.file_size / 2**20,
            data_path.stat().st_size / 2**20,
            feather_path.stat().st_size / 2**20,

5.6 Data Stewardship
Data provenance records the history needed to interpret and reproduce a dataset. A useful record names the provider, source, access date, selection rules, observational unit, temporal scope, transformations, and known limitations. It also distinguishes statements made by the provider from decisions made by the analyst.

File integrity can be recorded with a cryptographic hash. A matching hash shows that two copies contain the same bytes; it does not show that the data are accurate or appropriate for a question.

import hashlib

with data_path.open("rb") as input_file:
    sha256 = hashlib.file_digest(input_file, "sha256").hexdigest()

sha256

Responsible acquisition also limits unnecessary exposure. This public dataset does not identify the person who submitted a request, but it contains precise incident addresses and coordinates. An analysis that needs only ZIP Code or precinct summaries should avoid displaying individual addresses. Public availability does not eliminate the responsibility to minimize unnecessary detail and to follow the source’s terms of use.
Open-data curation requires more than distributing a readable file. Tussey and Yan propose six principles from their study of NYC 311: cross-organizational consistency, accurate data entry, efficient storage, current data dictionaries, automated quality assurance, and transparency (Tussey & Yan, 2025). Their examples include inconsistent representations of missing values, invalid ZIP Codes, implausible date relationships, unusual concentrations at particular times, redundant fields, and categories whose meaning varies by agency or period.
These findings are prompts for investigation rather than universal cleaning rules. A negative duration may reveal a timestamp error, a misunderstood field, or a clock convention. A concentration at midnight may be a default, a batch process, or a genuine operational schedule. A responsible analyst first quantifies the pattern, checks documentation and related fields, and asks the data curator when the intended meaning remains uncertain. Deleting or replacing an unusual value without that inquiry can hide the very process that needs to be understood.

A descriptive question asks which categories were most common among the selected requests. A comparative question asks whether the category distribution differed across boroughs or creation-time periods. A predictive question asks whether fields available when a request was created can predict a subsequent closure interval; it would require an evaluation on data withheld from model fitting. These questions concern recorded NYPD-directed requests rather than all illegal-parking events in the city. Domain knowledge identifies which differences matter to residents or agencies, while the intended claim determines whether additional data are necessary. The following table separates quantities that the extract can describe from the evidence required for broader operational, safety, equity, or reporting claims. The first and last questions can be investigated directly as descriptions of this NYPD extract. The operational questions require care because closure is an administrative event, not necessarily a field response. The safety and equity questions require the most augmentation: request counts alone cannot reveal how often a condition occurred, how many people were exposed, or how likely different communities were to use 311. The extract cannot support comparisons with agencies absent from the file.
Domain knowledge also helps choose a useful level of detail. “Where is illegal parking a problem?” is too broad because neither where, problem, nor the relevant measure has been defined. A narrower question might ask, “During the Labor Day week, which precincts recorded the most requests about blocked fire hydrants, and did their median closure times differ?” The revision identifies the unit, category, place, period, and comparison, while still acknowledging that the result describes recorded requests rather than all blocked hydrants.
A final evaluation applies the domain, measurement, scope, and evidence checks to the proposed claim rather than merely to its computational form. The records may show that requests created at night have different closure times from those created during the day, but the comparison does not establish an effect of reporting time: problem detail, location, staffing, and reporting behavior may also vary with the hour. Similarly, averaging ZIP Codes after they have been imported as numbers is computationally possible but has no geographic interpretation. Raw request counts by ZIP label describe the file, yet they are not comparable as per-resident reporting rates when areas differ in population and parking opportunities. Each proposed analysis must therefore name its measured quantity, eligible requests, comparison basis, and intended inference. A causal claim would additionally require a design and assumptions that address competing explanations.
Additional area-level data could supply denominators and context for ZIP-level request counts. Census characteristics are often tabulated for ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs), which are related to postal ZIP Codes but do not represent identical geographies (U.S. Census Bureau, 2023). The area-context workflow in Section 6.4 demonstrates one such enrichment and evaluates its key, reference period, join cardinality, and unmatched records. Even a validated match describes places rather than the individuals who submitted requests.

title: 5  Problem Formulation
text:
5.8 A Working Formulation
A working formulation puts the current choices in one place so they can be checked and revised. In this example:

Population: NYPD-directed illegal-parking requests created during September 6–12, 2026.
Outcome: the recorded creation-to-closure interval in hours.
Groups: Blocked Hydrant, Posted Parking Sign Violation, and Blocked Sidewalk, the three most frequent reported details.
Target: the closure-time distribution within each group, not a causal effect of the label or a citywide incident rate.

The group rule uses request counts from the same week but does not select groups because their closure summaries appear different. These choices give us the following working question:

Among NYPD illegal-parking requests created from September 6 through September 12, 2026, how did recorded closure-time distributions differ among the three most frequently reported problem details?

The working comparison has a defined unit, period, outcome, and group rule, but its interpretation remains descriptive. Groups were selected after inspecting the week’s category frequencies, and the records were collected through a reporting system rather than a probability sample of parking conditions. Location, reporting time, and agency practices may also differ among the categories. A difference between their closure-time distributions would therefore characterize these recorded requests during a holiday week; it would not identify the effect of changing a request’s problem label. Exploratory analysis can examine distribution shape and subgroup variation, while a later study could define a broader target period or collect process data to investigate the operational reasons for a difference. The present formulation makes those later requirements visible before a summary statistic or plot is chosen.
Other features of the checked extract support different formulations. The problem-detail table records 3,711 requests about blocked hydrants and 379 about blocked bike lanes, while 99 illegal-parking requests lack coordinates. These observations suggest several questions with distinct uses:

Which precincts recorded the most blocked-hydrant requests during the week, and how did their closure-time distributions differ?
Within each problem detail, did requests created at night have longer closure times than requests created during the day?
Were requests without coordinates concentrated in particular boroughs or problem details, and would their omission change a geographic summary?
How would the geographic pattern of blocked-bike-lane requests change if counts were compared with bicycle-lane mileage or another exposure measure?

The first three questions can be investigated within this NYPD extract, though the data cannot explain the cause of a difference without further evidence. The fourth requires an additional geographic dataset and a defensible match between its areas and the request locations. Each question concerns recorded requests rather than all conditions on the street.
The data-to-question route remains open after these examples. What other questions do the screened records suggest? Which would inform a specific decision or deepen understanding of NYPD-directed 311 requests? For each candidate, identify the observational unit, measurements, comparison, and claim that the available evidence could support. State what additional data or domain knowledge would strengthen the answer. ## Exercises {.unnumbered}

title: 6  Data Preparation
text:
6.1 Start with Source Data
Data preparation constructs an analysis table from acquired records while preserving the evidence needed to evaluate each transformation. The input in this chapter is the distributed NYPD-directed 311 archive and the scope defined in Chapter 5. Its principal output is a request-level table with documented field names, derived closure hours, a creation-time category, and matched Census area context where a valid match exists. The domain, measurement, scope, and evidence checks in Section 5.1 determine which fields are retained and which operations require justification. A successful transformation need not make every value regular: an unmatched ZIP label or an unusual timestamp can be a finding about the source rather than a value to overwrite. The workflow therefore separates changes in representation from new analytical assumptions, checks that request identity and scope survive each stage, and records what remains uncertain before the prepared table is used for exploration or visualization.
Data preparation starts from a question and a retained source, not from an assumption that the downloaded table is already analysis-ready. The previous chapter established the observational unit, checked the requested time window, and selected illegal-parking requests. Here, those checks become input conditions for the preparation workflow: scope assertions detect a changed or incorrect input, while later checks verify that transformations preserve the intended records. The chapter then standardizes representations where the meaning is clear, derives variables needed for analysis, and considers geographic enrichment only when units and geographies align. The steps are iterative because a transformation can expose a problem or show that a question requires different data.
A preparation plan separates three classes of decisions because they have different implications for the resulting claim:
Every class should leave an auditable record. Analytical choices especially require a rationale because they can change the outcome or comparison.
The original ZIP archive remains unchanged. Chapter 5 demonstrated its acquisition and initial profile; the code below repeats only the import, timestamp parsing, and row filters needed for this chapter to run independently. Temporary Feather examples in that chapter do not provide an input here. Each subsequent stage creates a derived data frame and verifies the assumptions that its operation introduces.
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

data_path = Path("data") / "311_nypd_lbdwk_2026.csv.zip"
requests = pd.read_csv(
    data_path,
    compression="zip",
    dtype={"Unique Key": "string", "Incident Zip": "string"},
    low_memory=False,
)

date_format = "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p"
for column in ["Created Date", "Closed Date"]:
    requests[column] = pd.to_datetime(
        requests[column], format=date_format, errors="coerce"
    )

start = pd.Timestamp("2026-09-06")
end = pd.Timestamp("2026-09-13")
parking = requests.loc[
    requests["Created Date"].between(start, end, inclusive="left")
    & requests["Problem (formerly Complaint Type)"].eq("Illegal Parking")
].copy()
The import block reconstructs the intended analysis scope without overwriting the downloaded archive. The half-open timestamp interval includes requests created on every day of the selected week and excludes those returned from the following Sunday; the problem condition restricts the subset to illegal-parking requests. The observational unit remains one service request, so a row restriction changes the eligible population but does not aggregate or validate individual observations. The explicit datetime format also exposes parsing failures as missing timestamps, which must be checked rather than silently interpreted as absent service activity. The resulting frame can still contain missing fields, unexpected category values, duplicate identifiers, or disagreements among geographic descriptors. Those issues require separate diagnostics before a derived variable or merge can be trusted. The subset also remains limited to NYPD-directed requests from one week, regardless of how consistently its columns are represented.
The checks in Section 5.4 profile the delivered extract before filtering, including its agency values, date boundaries, and missingness. Here, the scope report instead tests whether the reconstructed subset meets the preparation workflow’s input conditions: identifiers must be present and unique, creation times must fall within the selected week, and every retained row must carry the illegal-parking label. These executable invariants detect a changed input, altered filter, or parsing failure before derived columns are constructed. A failed check should prompt inspection of the source and preparation code, not automatic deletion until the report passes. This chapter remains independently executable while the substantive source diagnosis stays in the formulation chapter.
scope_checks = pd.Series({
    "rows": len(parking),
    "no missing request identifiers": not parking["Unique Key"].isna().any(),
    "unique request identifiers": parking["Unique Key"].is_unique,
    "all in intended week": parking["Created Date"].between(
        start, end, inclusive="left"
    ).all(),
    "all illegal parking": parking[
        "Problem (formerly Complaint Type)"
    ].eq("Illegal Parking").all(),
}, name="passed")

Coordinate completeness is not a condition for the ZIP-label merge below, because that operation uses the provider’s Incident Zip field rather than latitude and longitude. Removing requests without coordinates at this stage would therefore change the population for a reason unrelated to the planned join. A subsequent point map or distance calculation has a different eligibility rule and must report the resulting exclusions separately. An area match also cannot restore a missing point location: an area label identifies a region, while distance to a precinct requires a location and a specified distance metric. These examples illustrate why eligibility should be defined for each analytical quantity instead of imposed once as a generic complete-case filter.

Scope decisions select eligible observations and fields.
Representation decisions encode a recorded value for reliable computation without changing its documented meaning, as when a ZIP Code is stored as text.

6.2 Standardize Data
Standardization changes how values are represented so that they are easier to work with. It should not quietly change what the values mean. Common decisions include:

Dates: parse date strings as datetimes so that time comparisons and durations can be calculated.
Identifiers: keep ZIP Codes and request keys as strings. Converting 00501 to an integer would remove its leading zero.
Missing values: combine blanks, N/A, and Unspecified only when the source documentation supports treating them as the same kind of missing information.
Column names: create consistent analysis names while keeping a mapping to the provider’s original labels. Check for collisions because distinct source names can normalize to the same name.

These choices distinguish a representation change from a data correction. For example, renaming Created Date to created_at makes code easier to read; changing an unexpected date to a plausible one would alter the source information and needs separate evidence.
Category standardization requires evidence about the meanings of values, not only a preference for uniform text. The frequency table in Section 5.7 established which problem details motivate the working comparison. The following code inspects the distinct source strings before any recoding. The observed leading labels are interpretable, and apparent similarity between two labels would not by itself establish that they describe the same reporting condition. A data dictionary or curator explanation would be needed before combining categories with different names. By contrast, the code below changes column names to make operations easier while leaving category values unchanged. Keeping those two decisions separate preserves the provider’s distinctions and allows later readers to evaluate a proposed recode against the source.

detail_column = "Problem Detail (formerly Descriptor)"
observed_details = (
    parking[detail_column]
    .dropna()
    .drop_duplicates()
    .sort_values()
    .reset_index(drop=True)
    .rename("observed detail")
    .to_frame()
)

6.3 Derive Variables
Derived variables translate recorded fields into measurements needed for a question. Let \(C_i\) and \(L_i\) be the recorded creation and closure times for request \(i\). We calculate the elapsed interval in hours as follows:
\[
T_i = (L_i - C_i)/3600.
\]
The timestamp difference is in seconds, so division by 3,600 converts it to hours. The calculation is defined when both timestamps parse successfully and closure follows creation. It measures administrative closure, not officer arrival or the time when the reported condition ended. Keep the original timestamps so that a surprising value can be inspected and the derived value recalculated if needed. The name closure_hours describes the measurement more accurately than a name that implies a field response. The check below looks for issues before this value is used as an outcome.

analysis["closure_hours"] = (
    analysis["closed_at"] - analysis["created_at"]
).dt.total_seconds() / 3600

duration_check = pd.Series({
    "missing": analysis["closure_hours"].isna().sum(),
    "negative": analysis["closure_hours"].lt(0).sum(),
    "median": analysis["closure_hours"].median(),
    "maximum": analysis["closure_hours"].max(),
}, name="value")

A missing interval may result from a missing or unparseable timestamp. Do not fill it with an assumed closure time.
A negative interval conflicts with the expected event order. Inspect the source row and parsing before deciding whether to exclude it.
A large positive interval may be unusual but valid because an agency can close a request long after it is created.

The median summarizes the center; the maximum helps flag the upper tail for inspection. Chapter Chapter 7 examines the full distribution rather than removing long intervals with an arbitrary preparation cutoff.
The category “night” has no universal boundary. For this example, requests created from 8 p.m. through 5:59 a.m. are labeled nighttime; those from 6 a.m. through 7:59 p.m. are labeled daytime. The choice has consequences:

A missing creation hour remains unclassified rather than being assigned to daytime.
Grouping compresses 24 hourly values into two categories and hides within-group variation.
The groups do not account for differences across individual dates, such as the holiday in this week.

The original timestamp remains available for hourly analysis or a comparison using different boundaries. If the question concerns staffing or reporting conditions, use domain information to justify the boundary rather than choosing it only because the groups are convenient.

hour = analysis["created_at"].dt.hour
analysis["time_period"] = pd.Series(
    pd.NA, index=analysis.index, dtype="string"

analysis.loc[hour.between(6, 19), "time_period"] = "day"
analysis.loc[hour.ge(20) | hour.lt(6), "time_period"] = "night"

title: 6  Data Preparation
text:
6.4 Merge Area Context
An area-level merge attaches contextual measurements to requests, but only after we define how the geographic labels match. Here, each request has one row and each Census context row describes one ZIP Code Tabulation Area (ZCTA). A provider’s Incident Zip is a postal ZIP label; a ZCTA is a Census statistical area derived from address patterns. Equal five-digit strings allow a lookup, but do not mean the geographies have identical boundaries, and some postal ZIP Codes have no matching ZCTA (U.S. Census Bureau, 2023).
Before interpreting a merge, check these conditions:

Key: the context table has one row per ZCTA, so a duplicate lookup key cannot multiply request rows.
Match: the request ZIP label and ZCTA code use compatible formats.
Time: the Census estimate describes its reference period, which may precede the request week.
Unit: an area estimate describes a place, not an individual requester.

These checks make clear what the software joined and what the result means.
The supplied data/zcta_context.csv contains the 221 ZCTAs in NYC Open Data’s city list and their 2024 American Community Survey (ACS) five-year population, median household income, and household vehicle-availability estimates (NYC Open Data, 2026; U.S. Census Bureau, 2024b, 2026). It also records margins of error, an income top-coding indicator, the estimate year, and ZCTA land area from the 2024 Census Gazetteer (U.S. Census Bureau, 2024a). The provenance and conversion rules in data/zcta_context.md distinguish the Census estimates from the NYC boundary list used to select areas. These fields allow an analyst to check both the statistical meaning of an attached value and the geographic coverage of the lookup. The code verifies that each context key is a five-digit string, occurs once, and has the expected reference year before the merge. It then retains unmatched requests and reports them separately. The result is a documented link between labels, not an assertion that a postal area and its similarly named ZCTA have identical boundaries.
The lookup derives two measures from Census estimates:

Population density divides the population estimate by ZCTA land area.
Household vehicle availability is the share of households with at least one vehicle, calculated from the total and no-vehicle household estimates in table B08201.

Neither measure describes parking directly. Population density does not measure curb length or parking supply. Household vehicle availability does not identify vehicle ownership, registration, parking location, or illegal- parking behavior. The vehicle share is a ratio of survey estimates, and its sampling uncertainty is not calculated from the published margins of error. Both measures describe areas, not individual requesters, so the merge cannot support an individual-level or causal interpretation.
The NYC ZCTA selection comes from the zcta5 column of the city’s published dataset, as the following acquisition code shows. The chapter uses the saved CSV during rendering so that a live web request cannot change its results. The complete extraction, including the Gazetteer file and three ACS tables, is in scripts/build_zcta_context.py.

from io import StringIO

import requests

zcta_source = "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/35j5-n34v.csv"
response = requests.get(
    zcta_source,
    params={"$select": "zcta5", "$limit": 5000},
    timeout=60,
)
response.raise_for_status()
city_zctas = pd.read_csv(
    StringIO(response.text), dtype={"zcta5": "string"}
)["zcta5"].drop_duplicates()
len(city_zctas)


zcta_context = pd.read_csv(
    Path("data") / "zcta_context.csv",
    dtype={"zcta": "string"},
)
zcta_context["zcta"] = zcta_context["zcta"].str.strip()

if zcta_context["zcta"].isna().any():
    raise ValueError("The ZCTA lookup contains missing keys.")
if not zcta_context["zcta"].str.fullmatch(r"\d{5}").all():
    raise ValueError("ZCTA keys must be five-digit strings.")
if zcta_context["zcta"].duplicated().any():
    raise ValueError("The ZCTA lookup must contain one row per key.")
if not zcta_context["acs_year"].eq(2024).all():
    raise ValueError("The ZCTA lookup contains an unexpected ACS year.")
if not zcta_context["land_area_sqmi"].dropna().gt(0).all():
    raise ValueError("ZCTA land areas must be positive.")
missing_area = zcta_context["land_area_sqmi"].isna()
if zcta_context.loc[missing_area, "population_density_per_sqmi"].notna().any():
    raise ValueError("Population density requires a matched land area.")
if not zcta_context["share_households_with_vehicle"].dropna().between(0, 1).all():
    raise ValueError("Household vehicle shares must be between zero and one.")

# Match only syntactically five-digit request ZIP values. Do not silently
# pad or otherwise repair values that fail this check.
incident_zip = analysis["incident_zip"].str.strip()
analysis["zcta_match"] = incident_zip.where(
    incident_zip.str.fullmatch(r"\d{5}", na=False)
)

contextual_analysis = analysis.merge(
    zcta_context,
    how="left",
    left_on="zcta_match",
    right_on="zcta",
    validate="many_to_one",
    indicator="zcta_match_status",
)

if len(contextual_analysis) != len(analysis):
    raise ValueError("The area-level join changed the request count.")
if not contextual_analysis["request_id"].is_unique:
    raise ValueError("The area-level join duplicated request identifiers.")

join_report = pd.Series({
    "requests": len(contextual_analysis),
    "matched requests": contextual_analysis[
        "zcta_match_status"
    ].eq("both").sum(),
    "unmatched requests": contextual_analysis[
        "zcta_match_status"
    ].eq("left_only").sum(),
    "matched requests without land area": (
        contextual_analysis["zcta_match_status"].eq("both")

title: 7  Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
7.1 EDA Principles
Exploratory data analysis (EDA) examines distributions, relationships, and irregularities before a final account of findings is written. Its purpose is to learn what the observed data can show, what they cannot show, and which questions deserve closer investigation (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.). This chapter first states principles that apply across datasets and then develops them through a case study. The next chapter develops principles for choosing and evaluating visual displays across the data-science workflow; here, plots support investigation alongside numerical summaries and checks of the records.
EDA asks what patterns and irregularities are present in a prepared dataset, and which questions deserve more investigation. Three principles guide the work:
In practice, EDA cycles through a question, a calculation, an inspection, and a possible revision. A surprising value may send us back to the source; a group difference may suggest a better denominator or a more focused question. The calculation itself does not determine whether a pattern is important. Interpretation still depends on the eligible records, how the measurements were made, and what the analysis can support.

title: 7  Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Explore a question, not a plot collection. Preparation checks in Chapter 6 establish whether identifiers are unique and joins preserve rows. EDA then asks how an outcome is distributed, how groups differ, and which observations merit inspection. The same count can serve different purposes: missing coordinates may be a preparation diagnostic, while differences in missingness by borough may be an EDA question about which requests a map leaves out (Tussey & Yan, 2025; Yu & Barter, 2024).
Make comparisons fair. Center, spread, tails, missingness, and group size describe different features. A mean alone cannot describe a long right tail. Counts from two weekend days and five weekdays have different exposure, and copying one area income value onto many requests does not create many independent area observations. Choose summaries and plots for the comparison, then check that they tell a consistent story (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.).
Separate description from inference. A table can summarize every record in the defined scope. A test or interval asks what might happen beyond those records and therefore adds assumptions. Those assumptions need special care when the groups or thresholds were selected after examining the data. A result may also change under a plausible alternative time window, treatment of long durations, or geographic grouping. Such sensitivity checks show whether a conclusion depends on one analysis choice, but cannot repair undercoverage or confounding (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016; Yu & Barter, 2024).

title: 7  Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
7.2 Study Setup
The case study uses the screened requests from Chapter 6 to revisit the question in Chapter 5. The analysis proceeds in this order:

Describe the full distribution of recorded closure hours.
Compare the three most frequently reported problem-detail groups. The frequency rule is set before examining their closure summaries, but it does not make the groups random or comparable in other respects.
Examine variation by detail, creation date, borough, and matched area to see what a citywide median might hide.
Use a permutation calculation and bootstrap interval to illustrate how inference adds assumptions, then check sensitivity to selected analysis choices.

At each step, the four formulation checks in Section 5.1 limit what the observed differences can establish.
The initial scope report provides an audit of the table that enters this analysis rather than a second lesson in import and cleaning. The shared preparation function applies the documented time and problem filters, timestamp parsing, field names, and closure-time definition from Chapter 6. The report then verifies the number of request identifiers, missing or negative outcomes, and missing coordinates that affect later spatial comparisons. These checks establish the eligible set for the present figures; they do not resolve whether reporting behavior or agency practice differs across groups. The order of analysis is deliberate: inspect the overall distribution, apply the frequency-based group rule, examine time and place, and only then consider inferential and sensitivity calculations. This order makes it possible to distinguish a comparison specified by the working formulation from an additional pattern noticed during exploration.

7.3 Closure Time by Detail
The overall closure-time distribution establishes which summaries can represent a typical request and which features require separate attention. The median divides observed intervals into lower and upper halves, while a quantile identifies a specified fraction of intervals at or below its value. The mean reflects every recorded duration and is more sensitive to the long upper tail. Reporting these quantities together allows readers to distinguish a typical interval from delayed closures rather than reducing both to one number.     "treatment"
)["cases"].sum()
result = pd.concat([within_risk, pooled.rename("Pooled").to_frame().T])

result["B case share"] = case_shares["B"]
result.loc["Pooled", ["A case share", "B case share"]] = 1

title: 7  Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
7.5 Uncertainty Assessment
A hypothesis test can be part of EDA when its assumptions and limited purpose are explicit. Consider the median closure-time difference between Blocked Hydrant and Blocked Sidewalk requests. For the observed week, that difference is descriptive and needs no test. A test addresses a different question: under a model in which requests from the two detail groups have exchangeable closure-time distributions, how unusual would the observed difference be? The permutation calculation below pools the two groups and reallocates their labels while preserving their sizes. Its two-sided statistic is the absolute difference between medians. A bootstrap interval separately resamples requests within each group to show variability under an independent-request model.
The appropriate test depends on the outcome scale, comparison structure, and sampling or assignment process. The table links common questions to Python functions and states the null or design condition each function addresses (SciPy Developers, 2026; statsmodels Developers, 2026b, 2026a). This guide is not an automatic decision rule: inspect the data and define the target contrast before choosing a test (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.).








Question and design
Test and Python function
Null or key condition




Is one numerical mean equal to a reference value?
One-sample \(t\) test, scipy.stats.ttest_1samp
Population mean equals the reference value.


Do two independent groups have different means?
Welch \(t\) test, scipy.stats.ttest_ind(..., equal_var=False)
Population means are equal; equal variances are not assumed.


Do paired measurements have different means?
Paired \(t\) test, scipy.stats.ttest_rel
Mean within-pair difference is zero; pairs are independent.


Do three or more independent groups have equal means?
One-way ANOVA, scipy.stats.f_oneway; use equal_var=False for Welch ANOVA
All group means are equal; classical ANOVA assumes equal variances, and follow-up comparisons need multiplicity control.


Are two categorical variables associated?
Chi-square test, scipy.stats.chi2_contingency
Variables are independent; the large-sample approximation must be adequate.


Is a sparse \(2\times2\) table associated?
Fisher exact test, scipy.stats.fisher_exact
Tests association conditional on fixed table margins.


Does one proportion equal a benchmark, or do two proportions differ?
Binomial test, scipy.stats.binomtest; two-proportion test, statsmodels.stats.proportion.proportions_ztest
Proportions equal the stated benchmark or each other; samples must follow the test’s independent-sampling design.


Do paired binary outcomes change?
McNemar’s test, statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables.mcnemar
The two paired marginal proportions are equal; pairs are independent.


Are two numerical variables associated?
Pearson, scipy.stats.pearsonr; Spearman, scipy.stats.spearmanr
Tests zero linear correlation or zero rank correlation, respectively.


Do independent groups differ in rank distributions?
Mann–Whitney, scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu; Kruskal–Wallis, scipy.stats.kruskal
Tests equal distributions or rank locations under their assumptions; neither automatically tests equal medians.


Is a chosen statistic unusual under exchangeable labels?
Permutation test, scipy.stats.permutation_test
Labels can be reassigned under the null; the statistic must match the question.



The first code example uses the contingency table from the three most frequent details to ask whether the observed detail mix varies by borough. The chi-square test evaluates independence, while Cramér’s \(V\) summarizes the strength of the association. The expected cell counts help assess whether the chi-square approximation is adequate. Because the details were selected by frequency in this same week, this is an exploratory calculation, not a confirmatory test of a prespecified hypothesis.

from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency

detail_by_borough = pd.crosstab(top["problem_detail"], top["borough"])
chi_square = chi2_contingency(detail_by_borough)
sample_size = detail_by_borough.to_numpy().sum()
cramers_v = np.sqrt(
    chi_square.statistic
    / (sample_size * min(detail_by_borough.shape[0] - 1,
                         detail_by_borough.shape[1] - 1))
)
display(detail_by_borough)
pd.Series({
    "chi-square statistic": chi_square.statistic,
    "degrees of freedom": chi_square.dof,
    "p-value": chi_square.pvalue,
    "smallest expected cell count": chi_square.expected_freq.min(),
    "Cramer's V": cramers_v,
}).to_frame("value")

The next example uses Welch’s test to compare arithmetic mean closure hours for hydrant and sidewalk requests. It answers a different question from the median comparison below, and the long right tail can make the mean sensitive to a small number of long intervals. The request-level calculation also assumes independent observations, although requests may share locations, times, or administrative conditions.

Requests from one week may share time, location, or agency conditions, which weakens a simple independence model. A statistical test does not correct those design limitations, and selecting a test after searching many groupings can make its nominal \(p\)-value misleading (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016). Rank-based tests such as Mann–Whitney and Kruskal–Wallis do not automatically test a difference in medians. Likewise, a bootstrap interval estimates uncertainty under a resampling scheme; it is not itself a hypothesis test. When many outcomes, subgroups, or alternatives are examined, report that search and do not treat a threshold such as 0.05 as a mechanical decision rule (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016).

hydrant = top.loc[
    top["problem_detail"].eq("Blocked Hydrant"), "closure_hours"
].dropna().to_numpy()
sidewalk = top.loc[
    top["problem_detail"].eq("Blocked Sidewalk"), "closure_hours"
].dropna().to_numpy()
observed_gap = np.median(hydrant) - np.median(sidewalk)

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
bootstrap_gaps = np.array([
    np.median(rng.choice(hydrant, size=len(hydrant), replace=True))
    - np.median(rng.choice(sidewalk, size=len(sidewalk), replace=True))
    for _ in range(2000)
])
interval = np.quantile(bootstrap_gaps, [.025, .975])
combined = np.concatenate([hydrant, sidewalk])
permuted_gaps = np.array([
    np.median(shuffled[:len(hydrant)])
    - np.median(shuffled[len(hydrant):])
    for shuffled in (rng.permutation(combined) for _ in range(2000))
])
extreme = np.count_nonzero(np.abs(permuted_gaps) >= abs(observed_gap))
p_value = (extreme + 1) / (len(permuted_gaps) + 1)
pd.Series({
    "observed median gap (hours)": observed_gap,
    "bootstrap lower endpoint (hours)": interval[0],
    "bootstrap upper endpoint (hours)": interval[1],
    "permutation p-value": p_value,
}).to_frame("value").round(4)

The observed median gap is about 0.865 hours, and the bootstrap interval is approximately 0.712 to 1.016 hours. The estimated permutation \(p\)-value is about 0.0005, with the added one in the numerator and denominator preventing a reported zero from a finite set of permutations. These results show that the observed separation is large relative to these relabelings and resamples. They do not establish that the detail label causes a closure-time difference. Requests may be related through place, time, repeat reporting, or agency practice, and the analysis was chosen after inspection of this week. The bootstrap interval does not include uncertainty from coverage, measurement, or group selection. A \(p\)-value should not be read as the probability that the null hypothesis is true or as a measure of practical importance (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016).
Sensitivity analysis quantifies how much a descriptive result changes under defensible alternatives to the primary calculation. Yu and Barter emphasize that choices made during cleaning, preprocessing, and analysis can affect a reported finding (Yu & Barter, 2024). The first check below restricts closure intervals to at most 24 hours to assess the influence of the long upper tail; it does not classify longer intervals as invalid. The remaining checks calculate the same hydrant-minus-sidewalk median gap within each borough, holding the outcome definition and group labels fixed while changing geographic composition. These are targeted perturbations of the eligible set rather than an exhaustive search for a desired result. The table reports group sizes alongside gaps because a large contrast based on few requests deserves a different interpretation from a similar contrast based on many. Neither sensitivity check removes confounding or extends the conclusion beyond the observed week.

def median_gap(frame):
    left = frame.loc[
        frame["problem_detail"].eq("Blocked Hydrant"), "closure_hours"
    ]
    right = frame.loc[
        frame["problem_detail"].eq("Blocked Sidewalk"), "closure_hours"
    ]
    return pd.Series({
        "hydrant_requests": len(left),
        "sidewalk_requests": len(right),
        "median_gap_hours": left.median() - right.median(),
    })

sensitivity = pd.DataFrame({
    "all requests": median_gap(top),
    "closure at most 24 hours": median_gap(
        top.loc[top["closure_hours"].le(24)]
    ),
}).T
for borough in sorted(top["borough"].dropna().unique()):
    sensitivity.loc[borough.title()] = median_gap(
        top.loc[top["borough"].eq(borough)]
    )
sensitivity[["hydrant_requests", "sidewalk_requests"]] = sensitivity[[
    "hydrant_requests", "sidewalk_requests"
]].astype(int)
sensitivity.round(3)

The all-request median gap is about 0.865 hours and changes little, to about 0.848 hours, after intervals above 24 hours are excluded. The geographic comparisons are less uniform: the gap is about 1.07 hours in Brooklyn and 1.09 hours in Queens, but only 0.10 hours in the Bronx and approximately zero in Manhattan. Staten Island has a larger gap, but its comparison uses only 54 hydrant and 34 sidewalk requests. Group sizes and possible differences in case mix or processing limit the interpretation of these contrasts. The pooled result therefore does not describe every borough equally well.
Exploration has answered the initial descriptive question for the recorded week: closure-time distributions differ among the three most reported details, with a long right tail and the largest median among Blocked Hydrant requests. It has also identified conditions for a more focused next analysis. A future question could compare those details within borough and creation-time strata across multiple weeks, while documenting changes in request volume and closure practices. A causal question about why closure times differ would require a design that addresses confounding and the meaning of the recorded outcome. The ZCTA analysis similarly motivates area-level questions but does not turn area income into a request-level explanation. EDA makes observed patterns and the limits of their interpretation explicit enough to guide that next question. ## Exercises {.unnumbered}
These exercises use the distributed request archive and, where indicated, data/zcta_context.csv. Report the record counts behind each summary, state units and exclusions, and distinguish descriptive findings from claims about processes outside the observed week.

 7.1 Examine whether long-closure requests vary by the hour when a request was created. Define a request as long-closure when its closure time is at least two hours; exclude requests without a usable closure time and report their number.

Divide creation hours into four six-hour intervals and state their boundaries. Construct a contingency table of interval by long-closure status, showing both counts and within-interval proportions. Include the eligible request count for each interval.
Repeat the table for the three most frequent problem details. Identify one contrast that changes across intervals and compare its group sizes.

Assess whether the direction of the area-level association is stable. Describe at least two limitations of a postal ZIP to ZCTA string match.



 7.3 Evaluate a proposed claim that hydrant requests generally take longer to close than sidewalk requests.

Reproduce the observed median difference, bootstrap interval, and permutation calculation using a documented random seed.
Repeat the median comparison within each borough with at least 50 requests of each detail. Report the eligible group counts.
Write a conclusion that separates the observed week’s pattern, inference under the resampling assumptions, and the unsupported causal claim.

title: 8  Visualization
text:
8.1 Purpose
Figures can help answer three different questions:
The same dataset can produce different impressions when the selected records, denominator, scale, or visual form changes. A figure is therefore part of the analysis, not decoration added after the calculation. The principles here also apply to prediction and model diagnostics in Chapter 9. Examples use NYPD-directed 311 illegal-parking requests from September 6–12, 2026, with maps and a small simulated dataset to illustrate design problems that the request data alone cannot isolate (Munzner, 2014; Wilke, 2019).
When no chart is obvious, work through four questions:
The code examples demonstrate these decisions. The exercises ask students to apply them to new questions and data sources while preparing for the midterm project. Examples build on course demonstrations by Sonia Lucey (Plotnine), Alejandro Haerter (GeoPandas), and Jack Perkins (Google Maps), and use files distributed with the book.
The question determines which information a figure needs to show. For example:
There is no one chart type for every purpose. During exploration, several views may reveal different aspects of the data. A figure for communication should make its main comparison easy to identify and retain the context that qualifies it. First specify the observational unit, measured variable, eligible records, and period from Chapter 5 and Chapter 6. Changing any of these changes the quantity being displayed.
The examples use the screened request table from Chapter 7, but each display has its own eligible set. The hourly and closure-time plots use all screened requests; the point map requires usable coordinates. That difference matters: missing coordinates could be concentrated in a particular borough or problem detail, so the map may not represent every request. The code below loads the shared table with the preparation function, creates time fields needed later, and reports the starting counts. It gives readers a concrete denominator to compare with later maps without repeating the import and filtering code (NYC Open Data, n.d.).
from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from matplotlib_inline.backend_inline import set_matplotlib_formats
from IPython.display import display
from plotnine import (
    aes, facet_grid, facet_wrap, geom_line, geom_point, ggplot, labs,
    scale_color_manual, scale_x_continuous, theme, theme_minimal,
)
from scripts.parking_requests import load_parking_requests, load_zcta_context

set_matplotlib_formats("svg")

parking = load_parking_requests()
parking["hour"] = parking["created_at"].dt.hour
parking["day_type"] = np.where(
    parking["created_at"].dt.dayofweek >= 5, "Weekend", "Weekday"
)

pd.Series({
    "requests": len(parking),
    "unique request IDs": parking["request_id"].nunique(),
    "missing coordinates": parking[["latitude", "longitude"]]
        .isna().any(axis=1).sum(),
}).to_frame("count")

The hourly and closure-time displays use the full screened table, whereas a point map must exclude rows without usable coordinates. The subset represented by the map could differ systematically if missing locations are concentrated in a borough or problem-detail group; marker transparency does not correct that coverage difference. An area map introduces another eligibility rule when it requires a five-digit ZIP label or a polygon assignment. Each caption should therefore name its eligible records, measured quantity, units, observation period, and any exclusion relevant to interpretation. These facts belong next to the display because the same source archive can produce different plotted populations. The locally held archive and its provenance are documented in Chapter 5; the remaining sections concentrate on how analysis choices become visible in a figure.

title: 8  Visualization
text:
8.2 Grammar of Graphics
The grammar of graphics provides a language for specifying how data become a figure. Its components describe the choices that connect observations to visible marks:

Data. The data component identifies the observations and variables used by a layer.
Aesthetic mappings. A mapping assigns variables to visual properties such as horizontal position, vertical position, color, or size; a fixed property is set independently of a variable.
Geometric marks. A geom determines the marks used to display the data, such as points, lines, or bars.
Statistical transformations. A statistical transformation summarizes or otherwise transforms observations before the geom draws them.
Scales. A scale translates data values into visual values, such as positions on an axis or colors in a legend.
Coordinates. A coordinate system specifies how mapped positions are arranged in the display, including the spatial frame used by a map.
Facets. Facets repeat a common specification across subsets of the data so that panels can be compared.

This decomposition makes a figure revisable: an analyst can change a mapping, geom, or facet layout without reconstructing the entire graphic. Wilkinson developed the general framework, Wickham formalized a layered implementation in ggplot2, and Plotnine implements that approach in Python (Plotnine Developers, 2026; Wickham, 2010; Wilkinson, 2005).
The first example compares the hours when requests were created on weekdays and weekend days. The study week has five weekdays but only two weekend days, so raw totals would give the weekday group more time to accumulate requests. For borough \(b\), day type \(d\), and hour \(h\), let \(n_{bdh}\) be the request count and \(D_d\) the number of observed days of that type. The plotted value \(n_{bdh}/D_d\) is the average number of requests per observed day in that hour. The code constructs it in three steps:

Count requests for each borough, day type, and hour.
Add any missing combinations with a count of zero. Without these zeroes, a line would skip hours with no requests.
Divide each count by five for weekdays or two for weekend days.

This puts the two day types on a comparable time basis. It does not account for borough population, vehicles, reporting behavior, or an unusual day in this one-week period.

borough_order = ["BRONX", "BROOKLYN", "MANHATTAN", "QUEENS", "STATEN ISLAND"]
hour_index = pd.MultiIndex.from_product(
    [borough_order, ["Weekday", "Weekend"], range(24)],
    names=["borough", "day_type", "hour"],
)
hourly = (
    parking.groupby(["borough", "day_type", "hour"])
    .size()
    .reindex(hour_index, fill_value=0)
    .rename("requests")
    .reset_index()
)
hourly["days_observed"] = hourly["day_type"].map(
    {"Weekday": 5, "Weekend": 2}
)
hourly["requests_per_day"] = hourly["requests"] / hourly["days_observed"]
hourly["borough"] = pd.Categorical(
    hourly["borough"], categories=borough_order, ordered=True
)

The Brooklyn figure demonstrates how a layered specification assigns a different role to each visual component. Hour is mapped to horizontal position, the normalized request count to vertical position, and day type to color. The line geom connects adjacent hourly summaries within each day type, while the point geom marks the 24 discrete hours from which those lines are constructed. A connecting line helps readers follow the temporal pattern, but it does not imply that requests were observed continuously between the hourly bins. The manual color scale assigns stable colors to the two categories, and the labeled horizontal breaks make the time scale legible without printing every hour. The code supplies a legend because color is mapped to a variable; changing a constant line color would not create a second group. Brooklyn provides a compact example before the same specification is repeated across boroughs. Readers should compare the timing and level of recorded requests, while retaining the one-week scope of the data (Heer & Bostock, 2010).

brooklyn_hours = hourly.loc[hourly["borough"].eq("BROOKLYN")]
hour_plot = (
    ggplot(brooklyn_hours, aes("hour", "requests_per_day", color="day_type"))
    + geom_line(size=1)
    + geom_point(size=1.5)
    + scale_color_manual(values={"Weekday": "#3366AA", "Weekend": "#CC6677"})
    + scale_x_continuous(breaks=[0, 6, 12, 18, 23])
    + labs(
        x="Hour request was created", y="Requests per observed day",
        color="Day type", title="When Brooklyn requests were created",
    )
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(figure_size=(6.4, 3.7))
)
display(hour_plot.draw())







Figure 8.1: Average requests per observed day by hour and day type in Brooklyn, September 6–12, 2026.





Faceting repeats one plot specification across subsets of the data. These two layouts answer related questions:

facet_wrap("borough"): each borough gets a panel, and color distinguishes weekdays from weekends. Compare the two time profiles within each borough, then scan across boroughs.
facet_grid("day_type ~ borough"): day type defines rows and borough defines columns. The panel position identifies both groups, so color is not needed to distinguish weekdays and weekends.

Both plots use a fixed vertical scale. A height of 20 requests per observed day means the same thing in every panel, though low-count panels can look flatter. Free scales make within-panel shapes easier to see but remove direct comparisons of levels. Choose the scale according to the question and state the choice in the caption (Plotnine Developers, 2026).

borough_facet_plot = (
    ggplot(hourly, aes("hour", "requests_per_day", color="day_type"))
    + geom_line(size=.8)
    + facet_wrap("borough", ncol=3)
    + scale_color_manual(values={"Weekday": "#3366AA", "Weekend": "#CC6677"})
    + scale_x_continuous(breaks=[0, 6, 12, 18, 23])
    + labs(x="Hour request was created", y="Requests per observed day",
           color="Day type")
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(figure_size=(6.4, 4.4))
)
display(borough_facet_plot.draw())







Figure 8.2: Average hourly request counts per observed day, with a separate panel for each borough.






day_borough_facet_plot = (
    ggplot(hourly, aes("hour", "requests_per_day"))
    + geom_line(color="#3366AA", size=.8)
    + facet_grid("day_type ~ borough")
    + scale_x_continuous(breaks=[0, 12, 23])
    + labs(x="Hour request was created", y="Requests per observed day")
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(figure_size=(6.4, 4.4))
)
display(day_borough_facet_plot.draw())







Figure 8.3: The same hourly summaries arranged by day type (rows) and borough (columns), with fixed scales.





Use the wrap when readers should compare weekday and weekend patterns inside each borough. Use the grid when separating the day types makes the panels easier to scan. Neither layout solves a limitation in the data: Labor Day falls on the Monday labeled as a weekday. The weekday line averages five calendar days, including a holiday, so it may not represent an ordinary workday. For a commuting question, the analysis would need a holiday flag, more weeks of data, or a narrower interpretation. A valid facet design can still compare groups that do not match the intended question.

title: 8  Visualization
text:
8.3 Comparisons
Choose a visual form that preserves the part of the data needed for the question:

Counts: bars should begin at zero because their lengths encode size.
Close estimates: aligned dots on a shared scale make small differences easier to compare.
Spread or skewness: show a distribution or an explicit measure of variation; a mean bar can hide a long tail (Cleveland & McGill, 1984; Weissgerber et al., 2015).
Change over an ordered variable: lines can show a sequence such as time. Connecting unordered categories can imply a relationship that is not present.
Groups and magnitude: hue can distinguish categories, while ordered lightness can show magnitude. Add position or labels when color alone may be difficult to distinguish (Crameri et al., 2020; Harrower & Brewer, 2003).

The closure-time plot compares the three details with the most requests in the selected week. Each mark has a specific meaning:

The dot is the median recorded closure time.
The line extends from the first quartile to the third quartile, covering the middle half of observed closure times.
The line is not a confidence interval. It describes variation among records in this extract, not uncertainty about a population median or a difference between groups (Correll & Gleicher, 2014).

This display makes group centers and middle spreads easy to compare. Use the empirical cumulative distribution in Chapter 7 when distribution shape or the extreme tail is the main question.

top_details = parking["problem_detail"].value_counts().head(3).index
top = parking.loc[parking["problem_detail"].isin(top_details)]
detail_summary = (
    top.groupby("problem_detail")["closure_hours"]
    .quantile([.25, .5, .75])
    .unstack()
    .rename(columns={.25: "q25", .5: "median", .75: "q75"})
    .sort_values("median")
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
positions = range(len(detail_summary))
ax.errorbar(
    detail_summary["median"], positions,
    xerr=[detail_summary["median"] - detail_summary["q25"],
          detail_summary["q75"] - detail_summary["median"]],
    fmt="o", color="#3366AA", ecolor="#666666", capsize=3,
)
ax.set_yticks(list(positions), detail_summary.index)
ax.set(xlabel="Recorded closure time (hours)",
       title="Medians and middle-half ranges by problem detail")
ax.grid(axis="x", color="0.9")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 8.4: Median and middle-half range of recorded closure times for the three most reported illegal-parking details, September 6–12, 2026.





Read the figure in this order:

Follow the common horizontal scale to compare the median dots.
Compare each line’s length to see how widely the middle half of closure times varies within that group.
Notice that the intervals overlap. The median ordering does not mean that individual requests in one group always closed sooner or later than those in another.

The plot leaves out group counts and extreme closure times; the table and cumulative distributions in Chapter 7 retain those details. If the audience needs to see delayed closures, use an upper-tail summary or cumulative plot. This is a descriptive comparison. Location, reporting time, and agency practices may differ among groups, so the visual gaps do not show an effect of the problem-detail label.

title: 8  Visualization
text:
8.4 Common Mistakes
Misleading figures can enter at several stages:

Selection: omitted records change the population shown.
Aggregation: a summary can conceal variation within groups.
Encoding: a scale or mark can exaggerate small differences.
Interpretation: a title can turn a description into an unsupported causal or citywide claim.

Wainer cataloged recurring ways to obscure data. Later studies examined how visual distortions affect readers and classified misleading figures in published work (Lo et al., 2022; Pandey et al., 2015; Tufte, 2001; Wainer, 1984). Reviewing only labels or colors will miss problems in record selection, denominators, or claims. Ask what conclusion a reader is likely to draw, then check whether the selected records and displayed quantity support it. Table 8.1 summarizes common mistakes, shows a deliberately poor example of each, and offers a repair check. The plots use the illegal-parking data or small simulated examples; their captions name the defect so the misleading design is not mistaken for a recommended one.



Table 8.1: Common visualization mistakes, their misleading examples, and checks for revision.
