Records without usable coordinates are dropped; the plot appears to include all requests.
Figure 8.5
Report the excluded count and label the figure as geocoded records, or use a field that supports the full eligible set.
(Lo et al., 2022; Tufte, 2001)


A bar axis starts above zero; small differences appear large in length.
Figure 8.7
Restore zero for a length encoding, or use aligned points when a restricted range is justified.
(Correll et al., 2020)


Panels use different scales without a clear cue; similar heights appear comparable.
Figure 8.6
Use fixed scales for comparisons of level, or state prominently that each panel has its own scale.
(Tufte, 2001; Wainer, 1984)


A mean or median appears alone; groups appear to have little internal variation.
Figure 8.8
Add a distribution, observations, or a defined interval suited to the sample size.
(Correll & Gleicher, 2014; Weissgerber et al., 2015)


Bubble area exaggerates a value; larger circles look disproportionately larger.
Figure 8.9
Encode magnitude with aligned positions or lengths, or scale circle area rather than radius.
(Cleveland & McGill, 1984)


A rainbow palette is used for an ordered measure; color bands suggest unsupported thresholds.
Figure 8.12
Choose an ordered, perceptually consistent palette.
(Crameri et al., 2020; Harrower & Brewer, 2003)


An area map shows request counts; darker areas appear to have greater illegal-parking risk.
Figure 8.13
Examine a suitable denominator and retain the count map for context.
(Openshaw, 1984; Robinson, 1950)


A title claims a cause or citywide trend; a one-week association appears to establish that claim.
Figure 8.10
State the observation period and measured quantity; separate description from explanation.
(Heer & Bostock, 2010; Tufte, 2001)






The first example drops requests without usable coordinates but gives the remaining counts a title that implies full coverage. This selection can change borough comparisons if missing locations are not distributed evenly. The repair should either use all eligible borough records or state that the figure summarizes geocoded requests and report how many records were excluded.

geocoded_by_borough = (
    parking.dropna(subset=["latitude", "longitude"])
    .groupby("borough")
    .size()
    .reindex(borough_order, fill_value=0)
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
ax.bar(geocoded_by_borough.index, geocoded_by_borough.values,
       color="#4477AA")
ax.set(title="All illegal-parking requests by borough",
       ylabel="Recorded requests")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=25)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 8.5: A misleading title implies that all requests are counted, although the plot excludes records without usable coordinates.





The faceted example uses borough-specific vertical scales without explaining that they differ. This makes the local peaks appear similar even though the request levels are not. Fixed scales allow level comparisons; free scales can help readers compare within-borough shape, but the caption and axes must make that purpose clear.

mistake_facet_plot = (
    ggplot(hourly, aes("hour", "requests_per_day", color="day_type"))
    + geom_line(size=.8)
    + facet_wrap("borough", ncol=3, scales="free_y")
    + scale_color_manual(values={"Weekday": "#3366AA", "Weekend": "#CC6677"})
    + scale_x_continuous(breaks=[0, 12, 23])
    + labs(x="Hour request was created", y="Requests per observed day",
           color="Day type", title="Similar hourly request levels by borough")
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(figure_size=(6.4, 4.4))
)
display(mistake_facet_plot.draw())







Figure 8.6: A misleading faceted plot: each borough has its own vertical range, so similar panel heights do not indicate similar request levels.





Baseline decisions should follow the visual quantity the reader is asked to compare. A bar represents a numerical value through its length from a common origin; when the origin is cut off, the apparent ratios between bar lengths no longer represent ratios between values. A line or dot plot primarily uses position, so a restricted range can help expose a small change if the axis limits are conspicuous and the plot does not invite an unwarranted comparison of physical lengths. Truncation can nevertheless alter perceived effect size across chart types, even when a visual cue signals the change (Correll et al., 2020). The paired figure holds the three median closure times fixed and changes only the horizontal limits. The left panel makes the differences occupy a larger fraction of the available bar length; the right panel restores the zero baseline required for a literal length comparison. Both panels omit the within-group spread shown in Figure 8.4, which is a separate loss of information.

medians = detail_summary["median"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 3.4), sharey=True)
for ax in axes:
    ax.barh(medians.index, medians, color="#3366AA")
    ax.set_xlabel("Median closure time (hours)")
axes[0].set_xlim(medians.min() * .85, medians.max() * 1.08)
axes[0].set_title("Truncated baseline")
axes[1].set_xlim(0, medians.max() * 1.08)
axes[1].set_title("Zero baseline")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 8.7: Identical median closure times with a truncated baseline (left) and a zero baseline (right). The left bars exaggerate differences in length.





Summary statistics can conceal differences even when the axes and scales are technically correct. In the following constructed example, both groups have a mean of two units. Group A contains three zeroes and two fives, whereas all five observations in group B equal two. The equal-height bars correctly display the two means, but they cannot communicate the different concentration and range of the observations. The point display retains the five individual values in each group and makes that difference visible. This example isolates information loss due to aggregation; it does not show that individual points are always the appropriate marks. Thousands of service requests would create severe overplotting, for which a histogram, empirical cumulative distribution, density display, or selected quantiles could better represent variation. The choice depends on whether the question concerns center, spread, tail behavior, or individual cases, and on how many observations can be displayed legibly (Correll & Gleicher, 2014; Weissgerber et al., 2015).

simulated = {"A": np.array([0, 0, 0, 5, 5]),
             "B": np.array([2, 2, 2, 2, 2])}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
axes[0].bar(list(simulated), [values.mean() for values in simulated.values()],
            color="#3366AA")
axes[0].set(title="Means only", ylabel="Observed value", ylim=(0, 6))
for position, (name, values) in enumerate(simulated.items()):
    offsets = np.linspace(-.13, .13, len(values))
    axes[1].scatter(position + offsets, values, color="#3366AA", s=35)
axes[1].set(xticks=[0, 1], xticklabels=list(simulated),
            title="Individual values", ylabel="Observed value", ylim=(0, 6))
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 8.8: Two simulated groups have the same mean but different observed distributions.





The next plot uses circle radius, rather than circle area, to encode median closure time. Because the area of a circle grows with the square of its radius, this choice exaggerates differences between the three problem details. A position or length encoding supports more reliable comparisons.

bubble_values = detail_summary["median"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
x_positions = np.arange(len(bubble_values))
ax.scatter(x_positions, np.zeros(len(bubble_values)),
           s=(bubble_values.to_numpy() * 30) ** 2,
           color="#4477AA", alpha=.65)
ax.set(xticks=x_positions, xticklabels=bubble_values.index,
       yticks=[], title="Median closure time shown by bubble radius")
for spine in ["left", "right", "top"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 8.9: A misleading bubble plot: circle radius is proportional to median closure time, so circle area exaggerates the differences.





Color and annotation should be evaluated by the comparisons they enable. Distinct hues can identify unordered categories; progressively ordered lightness can represent increasing magnitude; and a diverging scale is appropriate when a defined reference, such as zero change, separates two directions. An uneven gradient can create apparent thresholds where the data are continuous, while a distinction conveyed only by red and green can be inaccessible to some readers (Crameri et al., 2020; Harrower & Brewer, 2003). Decoration is not categorically harmful: experiments with embellished figures complicate a blanket prohibition (Bateman et al., 2010). The appropriate test is whether an element helps readers locate or compare evidence without implying an unsupported result. Every plot should also be reviewed as a claim. Its title should match the measured quantity; its axes and legend should state units; and its caption should identify the source, observation period, aggregation, and exclusions. When a figure is revised, the analyst should inspect the source records again to confirm that the repaired display still represents the intended population and denominator.
The final example gives one week of request counts a title that claims a citywide trend. The bars describe recorded requests in this extract; they do not establish a long-term increase in illegal parking across New York City. The repaired title and caption should name the observation period and avoid extending the conclusion beyond the available records.

daily_counts = parking.groupby(parking["created_at"].dt.normalize()).size()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.6))
ax.bar(daily_counts.index, daily_counts.values, color="#4477AA")
ax.set(title="Illegal parking is increasing across New York City",
       xlabel="Date in the one-week extract", ylabel="Recorded requests")
fig.autofmt_xdate()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 8.10: A misleading title turns one week of recorded request counts into an unsupported citywide trend claim.

title: 8  Visualization
text:
8.5 Maps
Maps require a choice of geographic unit as well as a visual form. This chapter uses request coordinates and polygons for the city’s 221 ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs) (NYC Open Data, 2026c):

A point map shows where requests were recorded. Points are approximate, may overlap, and may be missing for some requests.
A choropleth colors each area according to an aggregate value. It makes area summaries comparable but hides variation within each polygon.

Choose the map according to the question: where were reports recorded, how many matched an area, or how did an area summary vary? Population estimates from Section 6.4 can provide a denominator, but the resulting rate is requests per resident during the stated period. The map’s title, legend, and caption should name that quantity; request rates are not verified illegal-parking prevalence.
The map code must also identify how coordinates are represented. The request table stores longitude and latitude, so its points begin in EPSG:4326. The local ZCTA boundary file is derived from the official NYC source; its provenance note records the download and simplification. GeoPandas can transform between coordinate systems, but metadata alone does not prove that a point is located correctly.
The static city maps use New York State Plane coordinates (EPSG:2263). This projected system is useful for displaying the city and for calculations in linear units. Longitude and latitude are angular coordinates: a degree of longitude does not represent the same ground distance everywhere. A projection changes how coordinates are represented; it cannot fix a wrong address, approximate geocode, or missing location (GeoPandas Developers, 2026b).

zcta_polygons = gpd.read_file(Path("data") / "nyc_zcta_boundaries.geojson")
zcta_context = load_zcta_context()
with_coordinates = parking.dropna(subset=["latitude", "longitude"]).copy()
request_points = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    with_coordinates,
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(
        with_coordinates["longitude"], with_coordinates["latitude"]
    ),
    crs="EPSG:4326",
)
pd.Series({
    "requests in scope": len(parking),
    "requests with coordinates": len(request_points),
    "ZCTA polygons": len(zcta_polygons),
}).to_frame("count")








count




requests in scope
13040


requests with coordinates
12941


ZCTA polygons
221







A point map with many observations needs a display rule that accounts for overlap. Several requests can share a geocoded address, and opaque markers would cover earlier marks at the same or nearby positions. The following figure therefore uses a reproducible random sample of 2,000 geocoded requests and draws small, transparent points over ZCTA outlines. Sampling reduces the number of overlapping marks while preserving, in expectation, the distribution of locations among geocoded records. It also makes the plot unsuitable for reading exact counts at a location: the absence of a sampled point does not imply the absence of requests. Transparency helps show accumulation, but apparent density still depends on point size, opacity, and map scale. The polygon outlines provide orientation rather than an area-level measurement. A density surface would introduce further choices, especially a smoothing bandwidth and treatment of boundaries; those choices would need to be reported before the surface could support a quantitative comparison.

sample_points = request_points.sample(n=2000, random_state=2026)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 6.2))
zcta_polygons.to_crs("EPSG:2263").boundary.plot(
    ax=ax, color="#999999", linewidth=.3
)
sample_points.to_crs("EPSG:2263").plot(
    ax=ax, color="#225588", markersize=3, alpha=.3
)
ax.set_axis_off()
ax.set_title("Recorded request locations and ZCTA boundaries")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 8.11: A reproducible sample of 2,000 geocoded illegal-parking requests over NYC ZCTA boundaries, September 6–12, 2026.





An area map requires an assignment rule that maps each request to a named polygon or reports why it remains unassigned. Section 6.4 used equality of the provider’s five-digit postal ZIP label and a Census ZCTA code; it also explained why equal labels do not imply identical geographies (U.S. Census Bureau, 2023). Coordinates permit an alternative point-in-polygon assignment. That operation answers a different question, because it uses the recorded point rather than the provider’s postal label. It requires valid coordinates, a selected polygon file, and a spatial predicate. Under within, a point exactly on a boundary does not belong to either adjoining polygon, while overlaps can assign one request to several polygons. An imprecise geocode or simplified boundary can also change a near-edge match. Before shading a map, the analyst should count one-to-one, unmatched, and multiple assignments and decide which rule corresponds to the geographic target. The diagnostic below makes those outcomes visible for the supplied ZCTA polygons (NYC Open Data, 2026c).

point_zcta = gpd.sjoin(
    request_points[["request_id", "incident_zip", "geometry"]],
    zcta_polygons[["zcta", "geometry"]],
    how="left", predicate="within",
)
match_count = point_zcta.groupby(level=0)["zcta"].count()
pd.Series({
    "one polygon": match_count.eq(1).sum(),
    "no polygon": match_count.eq(0).sum(),
    "more than one polygon": match_count.gt(1).sum(),
}).to_frame("geocoded requests")








geocoded requests




one polygon
12892


no polygon
21


more than one polygon
28







The spatial diagnostic shows that 21 geocoded requests have no polygon match and 28 have more than one match in the compact boundary file. These counts establish that the join cannot be substituted silently for the provider’s ZIP field. A boundary point may fail the within predicate; overlapping polygons may produce multiple rows for one request; and boundary simplification can change a near-edge result. Each mechanism requires a different response. For a precise point-to-area study, the analyst should inspect the ambiguous records against the original boundaries, state a tie-breaking rule if one is justified, and report the remaining exclusions. The maps below instead retain the ZIP-label match introduced in Section 6.4, which keeps their area summaries comparable to the earlier data-preparation example. The point-in-polygon results remain a diagnostic of geographic disagreement rather than an unexamined source of replacement labels.
The paired choropleths separate the effect of a numerator from the effect of a denominator. For ZCTA \(z\), let \(N_z\) be the number of selected requests whose valid five-digit provider ZIP label matches its code, and let \(P_z\) be its 2020–2024 American Community Survey population estimate. The first map shows \(N_z\); the second shows \(10{,}000N_z/P_z\) when \(P_z>0\). Its unit is requests per 10,000 estimated residents during the selected week. The formula does not measure the probability that a resident experiences illegal parking, because the numerator consists of requests rather than verified events and the population is not the number of parking opportunities. It also combines 2026 requests with an earlier population estimate. Twenty-seven ZCTAs have a zero population estimate; their rates are undefined and appear in gray rather than as zero. A polygon with no matched ZIP-label requests can still contain geocoded requests assigned another label. Both maps use ordered color, but separate legends identify their different quantities and units (Crameri et al., 2020; Harrower & Brewer, 2003).

valid_zip = parking["incident_zip"].str.fullmatch(r"\d{5}", na=False)
area_counts = (
    parking.loc[valid_zip]
    .groupby("incident_zip")
    .size()
    .rename("requests")
    .reset_index()
    .rename(columns={"incident_zip": "zcta"})
)
area_map = (
    zcta_polygons
    .merge(zcta_context[["zcta", "population"]],
           on="zcta", validate="one_to_one")
    .merge(area_counts, on="zcta", how="left", validate="one_to_one")
)
area_map["requests"] = area_map["requests"].fillna(0).astype(int)
area_map["requests_per_10k"] = np.where(
    area_map["population"].gt(0),
    area_map["requests"] / area_map["population"] * 10_000,
    np.nan,
)

The next two plots illustrate the map-specific mistakes in Table 8.1. The first pairs a continuous rate with a rainbow palette, which can suggest abrupt boundaries that are not present in the data. The second presents counts as risk even though ZCTAs differ in population and other exposure. The count map can describe service workload, but it does not by itself identify where illegal parking is more likely.

projected_map = area_map.to_crs("EPSG:2263")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 6.2))
projected_map.plot(column="requests_per_10k", cmap="rainbow", legend=True,
                   ax=ax, legend_kwds={"shrink": 0.6},
                   missing_kwds={"color": "#bdbdbd"})
ax.set_title("Requests per 10,000 residents (rainbow scale)")
ax.set_axis_off()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 8.12: A misleading choropleth: the rainbow palette introduces strong hue boundaries into a continuous request rate.






fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 6.2))
projected_map.plot(column="requests", cmap="OrRd", legend=True, ax=ax,
                   legend_kwds={"shrink": 0.6})
ax.set_title("Illegal-parking risk by ZCTA")
ax.set_axis_off()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 8.13: A misleading choropleth: raw request counts are titled as illegal-parking risk, although areas differ in population and exposure.






projected_map = area_map.to_crs("EPSG:2263")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 3.5))
for ax, variable, title in [
    (axes[0], "requests", "Recorded requests"),
    (axes[1], "requests_per_10k", "Requests per 10,000 residents"),
]:
    projected_map.plot(
        column=variable, ax=ax, cmap="viridis", legend=True,
        legend_kwds={"shrink": .6}, edgecolor="white", linewidth=.15,
        missing_kwds={"color": "#dddddd", "label": "Rate unavailable"},
    )
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_axis_off()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 8.14: Illegal-parking request counts (left) and requests per 10,000 estimated residents (right) by matched NYC ZCTA label, September 6–12, 2026. Gray areas have undefined rates because their population estimate is zero.





Differences between the count and rate maps require substantive interpretation before they are treated as evidence of geographic risk. Residential population need not be proportional to the number of drivers, visitors, curb spaces, or people likely to report a problem. A commercial area with few residents can therefore have a high per-resident request rate without having an unusually high number of requests. Map color also depends on the chosen boundaries: combining ZCTAs into boroughs can conceal local variation, while a different grouping of neighborhoods can change the apparent association between location and requests (Armstrong & Wattenberg, 2014; Openshaw, 1984). Even a stable area-level pattern does not establish the behavior or exposure of individual residents (Robinson, 1950). A defensible map should therefore state the numerator, denominator, time period, assignment rule, and treatment of unmatched records. The analyst should also ask whether the geographic arrangement answers a question that a sorted table or dot plot could not answer as clearly.

title: 8  Visualization
8  Visualization
text:
8.7 Animate Change
Animation extends a static display by changing one part of the figure across frames. Matplotlib’s FuncAnimation repeatedly calls an update function, which changes the marks or data shown for the current frame. A useful animation keeps scales and spatial extents fixed, labels the frame in plain language, and changes only what the question requires. Animation can expose timing or accumulation that is difficult to see in a static figure, but rapid movement can also make comparisons harder. A static summary should remain available for readers who need to compare values across the full period. The examples use the week of illegal-parking requests to animate a borough count and the spatial distribution of recorded locations (Matplotlib Developers, 2026).
The first animation shows cumulative request counts by borough at the end of each day. Each frame adds a day of observations, so the bar lengths show how the total grows over the week. A fixed horizontal scale keeps lengths comparable from frame to frame. The animation describes request volume in this extract; it does not measure illegal-parking prevalence or borough performance.

import base64
import tempfile

from IPython.display import HTML
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation

def display_gif(animation, *, alt_text, caption):
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".gif") as gif_file:
        animation.save(gif_file.name, writer="pillow", fps=1, dpi=90)
        encoded_gif = base64.b64encode(
            Path(gif_file.name).read_bytes()
        ).decode("ascii")
        return HTML(
            f'<figure><img src="data:image/gif;base64,{encoded_gif}" '
            'style="display:block;max-width:100%;height:auto;" '
            f'alt="{alt_text}"><figcaption>{caption}</figcaption></figure>'
        )

daily_borough_counts = (
    parking.assign(date=parking["created_at"].dt.normalize())
    .groupby(["date", "borough"])
    .size()
    .unstack(fill_value=0)
    .reindex(
        index=pd.date_range(
            parking["created_at"].min().normalize(),
            parking["created_at"].max().normalize(),
            freq="D",
        ),
        columns=borough_order,
        fill_value=0,
    )
    .sort_index()
    .cumsum()
)

The update function redraws the horizontal bars for the date associated with each frame. The animation is saved as a GIF with Matplotlib’s Pillow writer; the file is created temporarily during rendering, so the figure does not add a generated binary to the repository. The FuncAnimation object remains assigned to count_animation while the GIF is written, which prevents it from being discarded before all frames are rendered.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
count_limit = daily_borough_counts.to_numpy().max() * 1.1

def update_count(frame):
    ax.clear()
    counts = daily_borough_counts.iloc[frame]
    ax.barh(counts.index, counts.values, color="#3366AA")
    ax.set_xlim(0, count_limit)
    ax.set_xlabel("Cumulative requests")
    ax.set_title(
        f"Requests through {daily_borough_counts.index[frame]:%b %d, %Y}"
    )
    ax.invert_yaxis()

count_animation = FuncAnimation(
    fig, update_count, frames=range(len(daily_borough_counts)),
    interval=700, repeat=False,
)
count_gif = display_gif(
    count_animation,
    alt_text="An animated horizontal bar chart shows cumulative request counts increasing across five New York City boroughs over seven days.",
    caption="Cumulative number of illegal-parking requests recorded in each borough by date, September 6–12, 2026.",
)
plt.close(fig)
count_gif

Cumulative number of illegal-parking requests recorded in each borough by date, September 6–12, 2026.


The map animation changes the points while retaining the same ZCTA outlines and projected view in every frame. Each frame displays requests created on one calendar day, using the coordinates supplied with the request data. The same geocoding limitations described for the static point map apply: overlapping locations can obscure one another, and an approximate point does not establish the exact location of an event. The display shows where requests were recorded, not how vehicles moved. It uses locally stored boundaries and does not depend on a live basemap, which makes the animation reproducible when the book is built.

map_points = request_points.to_crs("EPSG:2263")
map_boundaries = zcta_polygons.to_crs("EPSG:2263")
frame_dates = pd.date_range(
    parking["created_at"].min().normalize(),
    parking["created_at"].max().normalize(),
    freq="D",
)
min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y = map_boundaries.total_bounds
x_margin = (max_x - min_x) * 0.03
y_margin = (max_y - min_y) * 0.03

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 6.2))
map_boundaries.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="#999999", linewidth=0.3)
points = ax.scatter([], [], color="#225588", s=5, alpha=0.45)
frame_title = ax.set_title("")
ax.set_xlim(min_x - x_margin, max_x + x_margin)
ax.set_ylim(min_y - y_margin, max_y + y_margin)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_axis_off()

def update_map(frame):
    date = frame_dates[frame]
    current = map_points.loc[
        map_points["created_at"].dt.normalize().eq(date)
    ]
    coordinates = np.column_stack((current.geometry.x, current.geometry.y))
    points.set_offsets(coordinates)
    frame_title.set_text(
        f"Recorded requests on {date:%b %d, %Y} (n = {len(current):,})"
    )
    return points, frame_title

map_animation = FuncAnimation(
    fig, update_map, frames=range(len(frame_dates)),
    interval=700, repeat=False,
)
map_gif = display_gif(
    map_animation,
    alt_text="An animated map shows daily points for geocoded illegal-parking requests over fixed outlines of New York City ZCTAs.",
    caption="Geocoded illegal-parking request locations by day against NYC ZCTA boundaries, September 6–12, 2026.",
)
plt.close(fig)
map_gif

Geocoded illegal-parking request locations by day against NYC ZCTA boundaries, September 6–12, 2026.


The two animations make different comparisons: the bars emphasize accumulation, while the map shows the daily distribution of recorded locations. Neither should be read as evidence of a stable pattern from one week. The animation can direct attention to dates or places for follow-up; the static hourly, daily, and area summaries elsewhere in this chapter provide more reliable comparisons across groups. Students should state the frame unit, whether values accumulate or reset, the fixed scales, and the data excluded from each animation.
The same visual discipline applies when the course moves from description to modeling. A predicted-versus-observed plot can show where a model systematically overpredicts or underpredicts an outcome; a residual plot can reveal structure that an average error measure conceals. Neither plot is interpretable until the target, prediction unit, eligible observations, and evaluation data are defined. A plot of training residuals, for example, answers a different question from one based on held-out predictions. Chapter 9 develops that framework. The present chapter establishes the complementary visual procedure: preserve units, expose variation relevant to the question, label transformations and exclusions, and check whether the displayed evidence supports the claim in the title and interpretation (Munzner, 2014; Yu & Barter, 2024). These requirements make a figure useful across exploration, communication, and model diagnosis. They also give students a way to revise a first attempt: identify the inference the reader is invited to make, then inspect each data and design decision that supports it. ## Exercises {.unnumbered}
The exercises move from a specified comparison to a self-directed project question. Submit source code, rendered figures, captions, and brief written interpretations. For each figure, identify the row unit, eligible records, variables, visual mappings, source, observation period, and a limit on the claim. For a new NYC Open Data source, record its dataset identifier, access date, relevant data-dictionary definitions, and any filtering or aggregation. An attractive plot alone does not satisfy these requirements.

 8.1 Use the results of Exercise 7.1 to visualize how the proportion of requests taking at least two hours to close varies across the four six-hour creation intervals and problem details. Use the same threshold and eligible records; focus on translating the EDA comparison into a figure rather than rebuilding its contingency tables.

Use the three most frequent problem details identified in the EDA exercise. Construct one plot with color and one with facets. Explain which comparison becomes easier in each, and show the number of eligible requests behind the proportions.

title: 9  Modeling
text:
9.1 Frame the Prediction
Predictive modeling uses information available at a defined time to estimate an outcome that is not yet known. This chapter asks whether fields available when an illegal-parking request is created can help identify requests that will remain open for at least one hour. We compare request detail and borough with area context from the Census-linked table:
The analysis uses the same one-week, request-level data as earlier chapters. It predicts recorded closure time; it does not show that area characteristics cause a request to take longer or establish how predictions would perform in a different week.
The one-hour outcome connects the modeling question to the operational concern that illegal-parking reports may call for timely handling. It is an analytical cutoff, not a documented agency response standard. In the available week, 34.6% of requests with usable closure times were closed in under an hour, while 65.4% remained open for at least an hour. Recorded closure time is only a proxy for handling time: it may include dispatch, travel, queueing, reporting, and administrative steps. The analysis can predict this recorded outcome from observed fields, but it cannot isolate those processes.
Before fitting a model, specify what it will predict and what information it can use:
The one-hour cutoff is a modeling choice, not a documented agency standard. The density measure divides ACS population by 2024 Gazetteer ZCTA land area; the vehicle share is one minus the estimated fraction of households with no vehicle. These describe area context, not curb capacity or individual behavior. The ACS estimates cover 2020–2024, precede the request week, and have sampling uncertainty. We do not calculate the vehicle share’s uncertainty from the published margins of error.
The ZIP label links a request to a ZIP Code Tabulation Area (ZCTA), but the two geographies are related rather than identical, so this is an approximate match (U.S. Census Bureau, 2023, 2026). ZIP digits are labels, not quantitative predictors. A later benchmark uses the ZIP as a category to ask a different predictive question.
The prediction question is: among requests from this week, how well can the recorded fields distinguish requests that remain open for at least an hour? This is prediction within the observed setting. It is not a question about whether a predictor causes a longer closure, nor does it show performance in a future week. The four checks in Section 5.1 still apply: a model cannot repair an unclear target, an invalid measurement, an inadequate scope, or weak evidence.

title: 9  Modeling
text:
Unit: one illegal-parking request from the distributed week.
Target: one if recorded closure time is at least one hour, and zero otherwise. Requests without a closure time cannot be labeled and are excluded.
Prediction time: request creation. Closure time and later processing fields are unavailable then and must not be predictors.
Request features: problem detail and borough, recorded when the request is created.
Area features: population density, median household income, and the estimated share of households with a vehicle, linked through the ZIP label (U.S. Census Bureau, 2024a, 2024b).

title: 9  Modeling
text:
9.2 Establish a Baseline
A baseline sets a reference that a more complex model must improve. Because about two-thirds of eligible requests meet the one-hour target, predicting the majority class for every request already gives roughly 65% accuracy. That result does not distinguish requests: it labels every case as taking at least an hour. Accuracy alone would therefore make a useless classifier look respectable.
The analysis starts from the shared preparation function rather than repeating the import and filtering workflow from Chapter 6. It links the requests to the Census context already documented in Section 6.4, reports unmatched and incomplete records, and defines the binary outcome. It does not alter the source request data or rebuild the Census lookup. The train-test split reserves one quarter of complete requests for a final evaluation. Stratification keeps the target proportion similar in the two sets; it does not make the records independent or simulate a future week.

from scripts.parking_requests import attach_zcta_context, load_parking_requests

import pandas as pd
from matplotlib_inline.backend_inline import set_matplotlib_formats

title: 9  Modeling
text:
9.3 Use a GLM
A generalized linear model (GLM) relates a response distribution to a predictor through a link function. For a binary outcome, the response is modeled with a Bernoulli distribution and a logit link; this special case is logistic regression. GLMs also include familiar linear regression with a Gaussian response and identity link, as well as count models with a Poisson response and log link. The response distribution and link should follow the outcome’s scale and support, rather than being selected only because a software function is familiar (McCullagh & Nelder, 1989; Nelder & Wedderburn, 1972).
For request \(i\), let \(Y_i=1\) indicate that closure takes at least one hour, and let \(p_i = \Pr(Y_i=1 \mid \mathbf{x}_i)\). Logistic regression models the log odds as a linear combination of predictors:
\[
\log\!\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)
  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_k x_{ik}.
\]
The inverse-logit transformation maps any real-valued linear predictor to a probability between zero and one. Odds compare the probability of an event with the probability it does not occur. For example, a probability of 0.75 corresponds to odds of \(0.75/0.25=3\) to 1, while a probability of 0.5 corresponds to odds of 1 to 1. A coefficient describes a change in log odds, holding the other included predictors fixed; exponentiating it gives an odds ratio. An odds ratio is not a probability difference and does not by itself describe a causal effect.
The first GLM includes problem detail, borough, population density, median household income, and household vehicle availability. The three area measures are standardized across training requests, so their odds ratios describe a one-standard-deviation difference in the request-weighted feature values. The formula interface compares each categorical level with a reference category and holds the other predictors fixed. These coefficients describe conditional associations in the fitted model, not changes caused by the area characteristics (statsmodels Developers, 2026).

import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

glm_data = X_train.copy()
glm_data["long_closure"] = y_train
glm_formula = (
    "long_closure ~ C(problem_detail) + C(borough) + "
    "standardize(population_density_per_sqmi) + "
    "standardize(median_household_income) + "
    "standardize(share_households_with_vehicle)"
)
glm_fit = smf.glm(
    glm_formula,
    data=glm_data,
    family=sm.families.Binomial(),
).fit()

population_density_log_odds = glm_fit.params[
    "standardize(population_density_per_sqmi)"
]
income_log_odds = glm_fit.params["standardize(median_household_income)"]
vehicle_share_log_odds = glm_fit.params[
    "standardize(share_households_with_vehicle)"
]
pd.Series({
    "Population-density odds ratio per standard deviation": np.exp(
        population_density_log_odds
    ),
    "Income odds ratio per standard deviation": np.exp(income_log_odds),
    "Household vehicle-share odds ratio per standard deviation": np.exp(
        vehicle_share_log_odds
    ),
})

Each displayed odds ratio compares requests that differ by one training-set standard deviation in the corresponding area measure, while the other model features are held fixed. For example, an odds ratio above one indicates higher fitted odds of a one-hour closure for a one-standard-deviation increase; it does not say how many percentage points the probability rises. The context values repeat across requests in the same ZCTA, so area patterns are supported by 176 distinct ZCTAs, not by treating each request as an independent area. These are conditional associations, not individual-level effects or causal estimates. They also rely on a linear relationship between each standardized area measure and log odds.

title: 9  Modeling
text:
9.4 Check the Model
Model checks ask whether the chosen specification represents the observed relationships adequately. They differ from test-set evaluation: a model can fit the training records poorly, or fit them closely while predicting new records poorly. Logistic regression does not assume normally distributed errors or constant error variance as ordinary least squares does. Its assumptions instead concern the conditional Bernoulli response and the specified relationship between predictors and log odds. Residual and influence diagnostics can reveal unusual records or lack of fit, but no single diagnostic proves that a model is correct (Hosmer et al., 2013; Pregibon, 1981).
The current model makes several assumptions that can be checked only in part:

Each standardized area measure has a linear relationship with log odds.
The model is additive, so the detail contrast is the same across boroughs unless an interaction is included.
Sparse categories may produce unstable estimates.
Repeated Census values mean that area-level patterns are supported by 176 distinct ZCTAs rather than by the full request count.

Compare observed outcome rates with mean fitted probabilities across boroughs and across ordered groups of each continuous predictor, retaining the count in each group. Calibration is one check: predictions near 0.7 should correspond to an observed outcome rate near 0.7 among comparable requests (Calster et al., 2019).
The training-set summary below compares observed target rates with average fitted probabilities by borough. A large discrepancy can flag a lack of fit for a group, while close averages do not rule out errors for individual requests or interactions hidden within a borough. This is an in-sample check for the simple GLM, not an estimate of future prediction accuracy.

    requests=("observed", "size"),

title: 9  Modeling
text:
9.5 Evaluate Predictions
Evaluation asks how well the fitted model predicts requests it did not use for estimation or tuning. A training score is optimistic because the model has already adapted to those records. The reserved test set is used only after model choice; repeatedly adjusting a model after inspecting its test performance turns that set into another training resource and weakens the evaluation. Here, even a clean random holdout supports only a limited claim: it estimates performance for additional requests drawn under a similar one-week data-generating process.
Prediction metrics depend on the outcome’s scale. Numeric outcomes are evaluated by comparing predicted values with observed values; classification begins with class probabilities and applies a threshold to assign labels. The same train-test separation applies to both tasks, but their metrics answer different questions.

9.5.1 Numeric outcomes
For a numeric outcome, a residual is the observed value minus its prediction. Three common scores summarize different aspects of these residuals:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{MAE} &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_i - \hat{y}_i|, \\
\text{RMSE} &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}, \\
R^2 &= 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}
              {\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Mean absolute error (MAE) reports a typical miss in the outcome’s units. Root mean squared error (RMSE) uses the same units but gives large errors more influence because it squares them before averaging. The coefficient of determination, \(R^2\), compares squared prediction error with variation around the observed mean; a test-set value can be negative when predictions are worse than that reference (scikit-learn Developers, 2026c).
Recorded closure hours are numeric, so the held-out records also allow us to compare simple duration baselines. The training mean is the constant prediction that minimizes squared error; the training median minimizes absolute error. This comparison shows how numeric prediction metrics work without introducing a second fitted model.

from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

duration_train = model_data.loc[X_train.index, "closure_hours"]
duration_test = model_data.loc[X_test.index, "closure_hours"]
duration_scores = {}
for name, value in {
    "Training mean": duration_train.mean(),
    "Training median": duration_train.median(),
}.items():
    prediction = pd.Series(value, index=duration_test.index)
    duration_scores[name] = {
        "MAE (hours)": mean_absolute_error(duration_test, prediction),
        "RMSE (hours)": mean_squared_error(
            duration_test, prediction
        ) ** 0.5,
        "R-squared": r2_score(duration_test, prediction),
    }

9.5.2 Binary outcomes
For binary classification, a model often estimates a probability and then uses a threshold to assign one of two labels. The positive class is the category of interest, and changing the threshold changes the predicted labels and the resulting threshold-based scores.


9.5.3 Confusion matrix
A confusion matrix compares observed classes with the classes predicted at a chosen threshold. Its four cells count correct and incorrect classifications. A true positive (TP) is an actual positive predicted as positive; a false negative (FN) is an actual positive predicted as negative. A false positive (FP) is an actual negative predicted as positive; a true negative (TN) is an actual negative predicted as negative. The illustrative threshold is 0.5, so predicted probabilities at or above 0.5 are classified as positive. The displayed test-set counts use this rule and the layout in Table 9.1.
Each metric uses a different margin or combination of cells. The numerator and denominator make clear which errors a score counts:

Different fields use different names for several of the same ratios:

TPR, sensitivity, and recall all divide true positives by actual positives. They ask what fraction of requests that remained open at least an hour the model flagged.
PPV and precision divide true positives by predicted positives. They ask what fraction of flagged requests remained open at least an hour.
Specificity and TNR measure the fraction of actual negatives not flagged; FPR is the fraction of actual negatives that were flagged.
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It does not account for true negatives.

The complementary pairs TPR/FNR, TNR/FPR, PPV/FDR, and NPV/FOR each sum to one. The \(F_\beta\) score makes the precision-recall balance explicit:
\[
F_\beta = (1 + \beta^2)
\frac{\mathrm{Precision}\,\mathrm{Recall}}
     {\beta^2\,\mathrm{Precision} + \mathrm{Recall}}.
\]
The familiar F1 score sets \(\beta=1\). Values above one give more weight to recall, while values below one give more weight to precision; the choice should reflect the decision context rather than a universal preference (scikit-learn Developers, 2026c; Wikipedia contributors, n.d.).
Accuracy is the fraction of correct labels and can hide poor performance on one class when class frequencies differ. ROC AUC measures how well the model ranks positive cases above negative cases across thresholds; 0.5 indicates chance-level ranking and 1 indicates perfect ranking. AUC neither chooses a threshold nor checks whether probabilities are accurate. Log loss evaluates the probabilities themselves and penalizes confident errors. For observed binary outcomes \(y_i\) and predicted probabilities \(p_i\), it is
\[
-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[y_i\log(p_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right].
\]
These measures answer different questions and none is universally best (scikit-learn Developers, 2026c).
The threshold determines how missed long closures trade off against unnecessary alerts. The data do not specify the costs of these errors, so the example uses 0.5 only for illustration. A threshold selected for use would be chosen with training or validation data, then evaluated once on the held-out test set.
The baseline assigns every request the training-set target prevalence as its probability and predicts the majority class. The Census-context model one-hot encodes problem detail and borough, standardizes the three area measures, and fits logistic regression. The table compares their test metrics; classification measures use a 0.5 threshold. Since the positive class is more common, do not read accuracy alone. Compare it with ROC AUC, log loss, and the confusion matrix to see whether the model finds requests that close sooner or merely repeats the majority-class prediction.

from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    confusion_matrix,
    f1_score,
    log_loss,
    precision_score,
    recall_score,
    roc_auc_score,
)
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([
    ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical_features),
    ("numeric", StandardScaler(), numeric_features),
])
baseline = DummyClassifier(strategy="prior").fit(
    X_train[candidate_features], y_train
)

    preprocessor,
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000),
)
model.fit(X_train[candidate_features], y_train)

title: 9  Modeling
text:
9.6 Regularize Logistic Regression
The model has many coefficients because problem detail and borough are one-hot encoded, and the later ZIP-label model adds a coefficient for each observed area. Some categories are sparse, while the Census measures can be correlated. An unpenalized fit can assign unstable, large coefficients to these patterns and perform worse on new requests. Regularization limits coefficient size to trade a small amount of training fit for more stable predictions.
Logistic regression estimates coefficients by maximizing the Bernoulli log-likelihood. A penalty adds a cost for large coefficients:
\[
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_\lambda
= \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
\left\{
-\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[y_i\log(p_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right]
+ \lambda P(\boldsymbol{\beta})
\right\}.
\]
Here, \(p_i\) is the fitted probability for request \(i\), and the penalty does not include the intercept. The \(L_2\) penalty is \(P(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2\); it shrinks coefficients without usually setting them exactly to zero. The \(L_1\) penalty is \(P(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|\) and can set some coefficients to zero, producing a sparse model. Elastic net combines the two penalties (Tibshirani, 1996; Zou & Hastie, 2005). Since several Census measures may carry overlapping information, this example uses \(L_2\) regularization to stabilize the estimates without arbitrarily selecting one of a group of correlated predictors.
Scikit-learn’s logistic regression applies \(L_2\) regularization by default. Its C parameter is inversely related to the penalty strength, so smaller values apply stronger shrinkage (scikit-learn Developers, 2026b). Numeric predictors must be standardized because the penalty acts on coefficient size; otherwise, a change in measurement units changes how strongly a predictor is penalized. The analysis standardizes the area measures and keeps preprocessing inside the cross-validation pipeline.
Cross-validation selects C using training data alone. Within each fold, the pipeline learns its scaling, category encoding, and model coefficients from the fold’s training records, then evaluates log loss on its validation records. The candidate with the lowest mean validation log loss is refitted on the complete training set. The separate test set remains untouched until selection is complete because using the same cross-validation scores both to select and report final performance can be optimistic (scikit-learn Developers, 2026a; Varma & Simon, 2006).
The comparison separates measured area context from a postal-code lookup. All four models use the same training and test requests. One model uses problem detail and borough; a second adds three ACS-derived area measures; a third adds the incident ZIP label as a categorical identifier; and a fourth uses a smoothed target encoding of that label. Five-fold stratified cross-validation selects C by log loss, a probability-focused criterion. Standardization and one-hot encoding are inside the pipeline so each fold learns its preprocessing from its own training portion. The ZIP-label model is a predictive benchmark for areas already represented in the data; its coefficient for a ZIP label does not explain what neighborhood feature may relate to closure time.
One-hot encoding gives each ZIP label its own coefficient, which can be unstable when some labels have few requests. Smoothed target encoding offers another representation: it replaces a label with an estimate of its one-hour closure rate, then shrinks that estimate toward the overall rate. For ZCTA \(j\), a common estimate is
\[
  \widetilde{p}_j =
  \frac{s_j + \alpha \bar{p}}{n_j + \alpha},
\]
where \(s_j\) is the number of one-hour closures in ZCTA \(j\), \(n_j\) is its number of requests, \(\bar{p}\) is the overall training-set rate, and \(\alpha\) controls shrinkage. Larger values of \(\alpha\) pull area estimates more strongly toward the overall rate. This empirical Bayes idea is useful for categories with different sample sizes (Micci-Barreca, 2001; Pargent et al., 2022). Since the encoding uses the outcome, fitting it on each row’s own outcome would leak information into the training data. The encoder below cross-fits the training values within each training fold; for the held-out test set, it uses category rates estimated from the full training set (scikit-learn Developers, 2026d).

from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.preprocessing import TargetEncoder

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=2026)
candidate_C = {"logisticregression__C": [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}

def tune_logistic(categorical, numeric):
    transformers = []
    if categorical:
        transformers.append((
            "categorical",
            OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"),
            categorical,
        ))
    if numeric:
        transformers.append(("numeric", StandardScaler(), numeric))
    encoder = ColumnTransformer(transformers)
    pipeline = make_pipeline(
        encoder,
        LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000),
    )
    search = GridSearchCV(
        pipeline,
        candidate_C,
        scoring="neg_log_loss",
        cv=cv,
        refit=True,
    )
    features = categorical + numeric
    search.fit(X_train[features], y_train)
    probability = search.predict_proba(X_test[features])[:, 1]
    return search, probability

zip_identifier_features = categorical_features + ["incident_zip"]
detail_borough_search, detail_borough_probability = tune_logistic(
    categorical_features, []
)
census_search, census_probability = tune_logistic(
    categorical_features, numeric_features
)
zip_id_search, zip_id_probability = tune_logistic(
    zip_identifier_features, []
)

zip_target_pipeline = make_pipeline(
    ColumnTransformer([
        ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical_features),
        (
            "zip_target",
            TargetEncoder(
                target_type="binary",
                cv=StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=2026),
            ),
            ["incident_zip"],
        ),
    ]),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000),
)
zip_target_search = GridSearchCV(
    zip_target_pipeline,
    {
        "columntransformer__zip_target__smooth": [1, 10, 100],
        "logisticregression__C": [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10],
    },
    scoring="neg_log_loss",
    cv=cv,
    refit=True,
)
zip_target_features = categorical_features + ["incident_zip"]
zip_target_search.fit(X_train[zip_target_features], y_train)
zip_target_probability = zip_target_search.predict_proba(
    X_test[zip_target_features]
)[:, 1]

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "Detail and borough": score_predictions(detail_borough_probability),
    "Census area context": score_predictions(census_probability),
    "ZIP label identifier": score_predictions(zip_id_probability),
    "ZIP target encoding": score_predictions(zip_target_probability),
}).T
comparison["selected C"] = [

    census_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"],
    zip_id_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"],
    zip_target_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"],

comparison["mean CV log loss"] = [
    -detail_borough_search.best_score_,
    -census_search.best_score_,
    -zip_id_search.best_score_,
    -zip_target_search.best_score_,
]
comparison["selected ZIP smoothing"] = [
    None,

    None,
    zip_target_search.best_params_["columntransformer__zip_target__smooth"],
]

For this split, adding the Census measures changes test ROC AUC from about 0.577 to 0.589 and log loss from 0.636 to 0.631. The improvement is modest, but it indicates that the supplied area attributes add some predictive information beyond problem detail and borough in this test design. The ZIP-label model scores higher, with ROC AUC about 0.690 and log loss 0.593. Because the same ZCTAs occur in training and test sets, this score reflects area-specific prediction for locations represented in training. It neither identifies a cause nor demonstrates transfer to a new ZCTA or a later week.
Smoothed target encoding gives a similar test ROC AUC of about 0.688 and log loss of 0.595, with the cross-validation procedure selecting a smoothing value of 10. Three test requests have ZIP labels absent from the training set; the encoder assigns those labels the overall training rate. This comparison shows that a compact, partially pooled encoding can retain much of the ZIP-specific predictive signal in this split. It does not establish that ZIP-level outcome rates will transfer to future requests, and its learned category values should not be interpreted as neighborhood causes.
The Census estimates offer a more interpretable area-level question than the ZIP label, but they do not measure the mechanisms that directly govern parking or request processing. Population density is residents per square mile, not curb or parking-space density. Household vehicle availability is not ownership, registration, vehicle activity, or parking location, and median household income does not describe an individual requester. These ACS measures repeat across requests in the same ZCTA and carry sampling uncertainty; the vehicle share’s uncertainty has not been propagated. Only 176 ZCTAs contribute independent area contexts in this analysis. Direct measures of curb regulations, parking supply, vehicle activity, or precinct workload would be more informative for those processes. Any resource- allocation use would also require a separate review of measurement, fairness, and consequences for affected neighborhoods.
Regularization controls model complexity but does not replace diagnosis. The selected penalty can stabilize estimates while leaving omitted variables, measurement error, unfair performance differences, and domain changes unresolved. Area-level predictors also require validation that respects their shared geography when the intended use concerns new areas. The model’s intended use and validation design must therefore be considered together.

title: 10  Ethics
text:
10.1 Ethical Reasoning
Choices about questions, data, methods, and communication can affect people and institutions. This chapter offers a way to identify those effects, consider responsibilities, and document a decision. It draws on research ethics, professional statistical practice, and risk management, while recognizing that no framework replaces judgment about the setting. We use the NYPD 311 requests from earlier chapters as a case: public data can still raise privacy, equity, and accountability concerns.
Ethical analysis asks more than whether an action is legal or technically possible. Legal rules establish requirements in particular jurisdictions and contexts; professional standards describe responsibilities attached to practice; ethical reasoning also considers foreseeable benefits, harms, power, and the interests of affected people. A project may satisfy a data license and still expose a vulnerable person, produce a misleading comparison, or support a harmful decision. Conversely, identifying a possible risk does not by itself show that a project must stop. The analyst should specify the purpose, who is affected, what evidence is available, which alternatives exist, and who has the authority to decide.
Ethical review returns to the purpose, measurement, scope, and evidence checks in Section 5.1. These choices shape who may be affected and what consequences an analysis could have. Several frameworks offer useful, but different, starting points:
Use these six questions as a working review:
Return to these questions as the project changes. They do not produce an automatic ethical score; they make judgments and unresolved issues visible to collaborators, reviewers, and decision makers.

title: 10  Ethics
text:
The Belmont Report sets out respect for persons, beneficence, and justice for research involving human subjects. Keep its original scope in mind when applying its ideas to administrative data or nonresearch settings (National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research, 1979).
The American Statistical Association’s Ethical Guidelines address practice across data collection, processing, analysis, interpretation, communication, and model development (American Statistical Association, 2022).
A 2026 Journal of Data Science editorial connects trustworthy machine learning with fairness, privacy, transparency, robustness, uncertainty, statistical reasoning, and human judgment (Hicks et al., 2026).
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes risk work around governance, context mapping, measurement, and management (Tabassi, 2023).



What purpose does the analysis serve?
Whose data or experiences are represented or missing?
Who could benefit, and who could be harmed?
Which assumptions or uncertainties could change the result?
What safeguards or alternatives are available?
Who is responsible for the decision and its consequences?

title: 10  Ethics
text:
10.2 Purpose
A defensible project begins with a purpose specific enough to evaluate. State:

who needs the analysis;
what decision or understanding it may support; and
what uses are outside its scope.

“Improve safety” is too broad by itself. It does not identify an intervention, who would receive it, or what costs it could impose. Purpose also constrains data use: information collected to administer a service is not automatically appropriate for every secondary use just because it is accessible.
The NYPD 311 extract records requests directed to NYPD, not a census of illegal-parking events. A project might describe how these requests vary by time or location. That is different from identifying where violations occur, which neighborhoods are less compliant, or where enforcement should be increased. Each transition changes the claim and may affect residents differently. Before proceeding, the project team should state which claim it intends to support and whether that claim is compatible with the collection process and available evidence.
Affected parties include more than the people represented by rows. For this case, they may include:

people who submitted requests;
people whose vehicles or locations were reported;
residents and businesses in mapped areas;
NYPD staff and 311 administrators; and
decision makers who may rely on the analysis.

These groups can have different interests and different opportunities to challenge an interpretation. Consultation is most useful when it can change the question, safeguards, or decision, rather than serving only as approval after analysis is complete.

title: 10  Ethics
text:
10.3 Privacy
Privacy risk depends on context, not only on whether a table contains names. Precise locations, timestamps, rare categories, and external information can combine to reveal details about a person, household, or business. Removing direct identifiers may reduce risk, but it does not guarantee anonymity. Public accessibility also does not establish that every downstream use is expected, harmless, or consistent with the original collection purpose.
The distributed 311 extract does not provide a reporter name, but individual addresses and coordinates can still expose the location of a reported condition. A citywide count may need no street address at all; a neighborhood comparison may require only an aggregated geography. Data minimization asks the analyst to use and disclose the least detailed data adequate for the stated task. The appropriate resolution depends on the question, the population at risk, the possibility of linkage, and the consequences of disclosure.
The following example prepares a borough-by-detail summary without importing request identifiers, street addresses, or coordinates. It suppresses small cells in the displayed release table to illustrate one possible safeguard. The threshold is a teaching choice, not a universal privacy standard, and the internal count is not included in the table intended for release.

from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

data_path = Path("data") / "311_nypd_lbdwk_2026.csv.zip"
privacy_fields = [
    "Created Date",
    "Problem (formerly Complaint Type)",
    "Problem Detail (formerly Descriptor)",
    "Borough",
]
privacy_data = pd.read_csv(
    data_path,
    compression="zip",
    usecols=privacy_fields,
    low_memory=False,
)
privacy_data["Created Date"] = pd.to_datetime(
    privacy_data["Created Date"],
    format="%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p",
    errors="coerce",
)

start = pd.Timestamp("2026-09-06")
end = pd.Timestamp("2026-09-13")
in_scope = privacy_data["Created Date"].between(
    start, end, inclusive="left"
)
is_parking = privacy_data[
    "Problem (formerly Complaint Type)"
].eq("Illegal Parking")

cell_counts = (
    privacy_data.loc[in_scope & is_parking]
    .groupby(
        ["Borough", "Problem Detail (formerly Descriptor)"],
        dropna=False,
        observed=True,
    )
    .size()
    .rename("internal_count")
    .reset_index()
)

minimum_cell_count = 10
release_table = cell_counts.drop(columns="internal_count").copy()
release_table["requests"] = cell_counts["internal_count"].where(
    cell_counts["internal_count"] >= minimum_cell_count
).astype("Int64")
release_table
